paras: Reviewers mostly praise the hybrid for power, a roomy sweet spot and a plush, forgiving feel, and it suits players who want pop with usable control. Control is where takes split: Johnkew Pickleball and Farmer Lanky Pickleball found the pop demanding, while Matt's Pickleball called it the most forgiving of four paddles on resets. Weight also comes up, with Salt N Pepper Pickleball and Pickleball Studio finding the stock hybrid light and wanting more stability, while one Pickleball Playbook tester found it on the heavier side.

Reviewers mostly praise the spin, a large forgiving sweet spot and a light, quick swing, and suit it to intermediate players and up who want power with some touch. Control is where takes split: Pickleball Pursuit found it the hardest to control of the three paddles it compared, and Pickleball Studio found volley dinks lose energy at the kitchen, while DY Pickleball found dinks easy without added weight. Several reviewers add weight to steady it, and the Crystal Blue face is UPA certified only, not USAP, with JJ Pickleball noting that some buyers received patchy grit.

Reviewers mostly describe an all-court paddle for players who want heavy spin and grit that lasts, and Johnkew Pickleball, Pickleball Effect and Pickleball Playbook all report strong grit retention in their testing. Mixed takes come from feel: SupaSenpai found little dwell and called it a power paddle, while Rackets & Runners found it plush and control focused, with limited power and less stability on off center hits. Several reviewers also note it is approved by UPA only, and some add weight to the sides or corners for stability.

highlights.text: heavy spin and grit that lasts

paras: Reviewers recommend it mainly to players who want a durable surface, plus spin and stability on resets and dinks, with Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Effect both measuring little grit wear. Power is where takes differ: Farmer Lanky puts it at the bottom of the power category, Pickleball Effect places it firmly in the power category, and Pickleball Studio places it below the Bread & Butter Loco for pop. The swing weight draws repeated complaints, and Pickleball Studio and The Sweet Spot Pickleball both mention edge guard problems.

Reviewers praise it as a plush, forgiving control paddle for dinks, resets, blocks and third shot drops, and several recommend it to newer players or those upgrading from a basic paddle. Mixed takes come mostly from power and feel: Pickleball Studio and Dash Pickleball both rate power as modest, with Dash Pickleball noting it sits below thermoformed paddles, while Pickleheads found surprising power but an inconsistent sweet spot and a head heavy feel at the net. Version matters too, since Wongsquared and John Wilkerson liked the thinner 14 mm for extra pop, while Everything Pickleball could not tolerate it and prefers the 16 mm.

Reviewers praise the widest sweet spot of the line, a soft, dense feel and easy drops, dinks and resets, and Matt's Pickleball and The Pickleball Dad both point most players to the Pegasus first. The main complaint is power: Pickleball Studio says the player must supply all of it, Pickleball Effect measured the lowest firepower in the line, and Nikki Maldonado finds drives and flicks need extra effort. Pickleball Playbook calls the power muted but adequate and finds the sweet spot easier to hit than on the 11SIX24 Hurache-X Jelly Bean 2, and several reviewers note the line is UPAA certified only.

highlights.text: widest sweet spot of the line
the player must supply all of it

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as a forgiving widebody with a very large sweet spot, easy control and hex grit spin that several say has held up. Drill More Pickleball rated it B tier and found it too poppy at the kitchen, Pickleball Tech Dude described a dead zone above the corners where shots drift, and Pickleball Effect measured the lowest pop of the four Power 2 shapes. Several reviewers put power at the low end of the line, and Spinwave Pickleball and Pickleball Adventure both note it is not approved for USA Pickleball sanctioned play.

Reviewers praise elite, long-lasting HexGrit spin and easy power, and Pickleball Playbook and Pickleheads point it at intermediate and better players. Mixed takes come from control and the soft game: Matt's Pickleball scored its control lowest of three paddles, Pickleball On Call called the sweet spot hit or miss, and Pickleball Playbook Paddles found resets harder until weight was added. Several reviewers also note it is not USAP approved, while Matthew K Pickleball found the launch angle forgiving and needed no added weight.

highlights.text: resets harder until weight was added

paras: Reviewers praise the elite spin from the hex grit face, which several wear tests found lost very little over long use, and a light, quick hybrid shape that takes added weight well. Takes differ on feel and control: Pickleball On Call calls it muted and mushy with a hit or miss sweet spot, and Pickleball Tech Dude finds a dead zone near the top, while Pickleball Effect and Pickleball Playbook find the sweet spot big, and Pickleball Studio notes slightly more misses than expected on dinks and thirds. Many reviewers also point out it is UPAA approved only, so it may be refused at events that require USAP approval.

highlights.text: elite spin from the hex grit face

paras: Reviewers mostly recommend the Honolulu J6CR to intermediate and advanced players who want a light, fast elongated paddle with strong spin and a large sweet spot. Power is where takes differ: Pickleheads rates it among the best they have seen, while Pickleball Studio calls it mid-tier and Ignatowich HQ finds it good but not great. Several reviewers, including Smash Pickleball and Pickleball Effect, preferred it with added weight, since the stock swing weight is low.

highlights.text: strong spin and a large sweet spot

paras: Pickleheads, PickleballVN 365 and Pickleball Union praise the power, pop and spin, and several reviewers recommend it mainly to intermediate and advanced players because it is easy to overhit. Opinions on thickness split: MyPicklevn, PickleballVN 365 and Pickleball Medicine find the 16mm steadier and easier to control, while Rackets & Runners and Pickleball Studio prefer the 14mm for predictable resets and depth control. Durability is the open question: Pickleheads points to a history of propulsion core breakdown and Pickleball Medicine says it is too soon to judge.

highlights.text: praise the power, pop and spin

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the Pulse line for a large, forgiving sweet spot and easy touch shots, with the V and S usually placed in the all court group. Mixed takes come from power and break-in: The Pickleball Wise found the S Hybrid short on power for finishing easy balls and rated it Mixed, Tickle My Pickleball only had a few games on the curved hybrid, and reviewers disagree on whether the paddles get hotter, soften or barely change with play. Labels also vary, with Pickleball Medicine calling the series the best for control while DDOG_Pickleball calls the S firmly all court.

highlights.text: short on power for finishing easy balls

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the power and pop, with Pickleball Studio, Amir's Pickleball and Your Pickleball Partner placing it at or near the top of what is legal, and many calling the spin elite. Mixed takes mostly come from the small sweet spot, which West Side Pickleball and Ignatowich HQ found unforgiving off center, and several reviewers added tape or weight with only partial help. Spin is less settled, since Pickleball Blast and Rackets & Runners found the grit smoother than the Six Zero Ruby Pro, while Matt's Pickleball and All Drive No Drop Pickleball reported no grit loss over extended play.

Reviewers such as Womack Pickleball and Tickle My Pickleball praise it as an all-court paddle with a good sweet spot, high spin and a controlled feel that suits resets and dinks. Mixed takes come from power and feel: Pickleball Rx finds power muted on big serves and drives, Smash Pickleball finds it too soft and mushy to read the ball, and Famous by Friday Pickleball calls the sweet spot very small with a stiff feel, which runs against the larger sweet spot described by Matt's Pickleball and Pickleheads. Several reviewers also place it below the Selkirk Boomstik on firepower.

highlights.text: power muted on big serves and drives

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as an all court paddle with a wide sweet spot and high spin, and Cliff Pickleball rated its control 10 out of 10. Takes differ on power versus control: Pickleball Studio calls it a power paddle despite the control label, while Pickleball Effect found it stiffer and less plush until lead tape was added. Pickleball Blast and Pickleheads also found the handle slippery when sweaty and suggested an overgrip.

highlights.text: wide sweet spot and high spin

paras: Reviewers praise the extreme grit and spin plus controllable touch, with Matthew K Pickleball finding feel and control that nothing tops and Pickleball Will finding it more intuitive than the Six Zero Black Opal 14mm. Takes split on the sweet spot: Famous by Friday Pickleball and STS PICKLEBALL find it large for a polypropylene paddle, while West Side Pickleball, Womack Pickleball and The Honest Take found it small. Womack Pickleball was the one reviewer who did not recommend it, citing a stiff feel and a drop in pop when missing the center.

Reviewers mostly praise the Six Zero Ruby for strong spin, a plush Kevlar feel and a large sweet spot, and many call it a good fit for all court players who can give up some pop. Pop is where takes split: Rackets & Runners found slightly less pop than the Six Zero Double Black Diamond Control, while Pickleheads found more. Durability is the other open question, as Pickleball Pursuit measured a drop in spin after about 3 to 4 hours, while several others said surface life was still unproven.

Reviewers praise the low swing weight, the large sweet spot and the spin from the Kevlar face, and describe a widebody that blocks and resets yet has more pop than a control paddle suggests. The main split is against the Volair Mach 2 Forza: Pickleball Medicine, STS PICKLEBALL and Pickleball Pursuit find the Apollo poppier but a little less controllable, while Pickleball Studio reports vibration in stock form and says it needs lead tape to reach its potential. Tickle My Pickleball names the shorter length as the main downside, and Pickleball Pursuit dislikes the grip inserts that stick out past the paddle width.

Reviewers mostly describe a soft, plush all-court paddle that suits players wanting more power than the Vatic Pro Prism Flash, with good spin and a non-thermoformed build. Mixed takes come from weight and control: Unforced Errors PB found the 16 mm Flash head heavy and too slow at the kitchen, and Pickleheads rated its control below the Vatic Pro Prism Flash. Most 16 mm testers call pop low, while BP2 Pickleball and InfoTechYeti found the 14 mm versions poppier.

highlights.text: head heavy and too slow at the kitchen

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as good value for control players and for newer to intermediate players, with easy drops and resets and a large sweet spot. Takes split on pop and stability: STS Pickleball and Muller Pickleball found lively pop, Entre Palas Pickleball described it as lacking raw pop, and Pickle Li and Matt's Pickleball found resets popping up or stock play inconsistent until weight was added. Pickleheads also reported mishit feedback in the arm, and several reviewers noted the grit wears down.

Reviewers mostly praise the heavy spin and grit that held up over long testing, and the paddle suits aggressive players, singles players and two-handed backhand users who want reach from the 6 inch handle. Mixed takes come from forgiveness and feel: Paddle Review Hub and Pickleball Effect call it the least forgiving Power 2 shape, STS Pickleball finds control a good bit below average so rushed dinks can float, and Martin Grunin Pickleball found less pop at the top of the face. Against the 11SIX24 Vapor Power 2, Francis Rances Pickleball picks this one for faster hands in the kitchen, while Pickleball Tech Dude still prefers the Vapor Power 2.

highlights.text: less pop at the top of the face

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the Loco Elongated as the power shape, with a sweet spot they call good for an elongated, and it suits drivers who want reach. Mixed takes come from weight and touch: STS Pickleball and Johnkew Pickleball found the stock swing weight high, Matt's Pickleball said the low twist weight needs cleaner contact, and The Adventurous Boomer found it less plush on drops and resets than the Standard and Hybrid shapes. Grit durability is split too, as Maiko and West Side Pickleball saw it wear, while STS Pickleball said it held up over two months.

highlights.text: found the stock swing weight high

paras: Reviewers praise the big, forgiving sweet spot and quick hands, and Pickleball Nation, Matt's Pickleball and STS PICKLEBALL single out the standard shape for speed or forgiveness. Johnkew Pickleball struggled to control the pop on midcourt resets and Jordan Plays Pickle says the kitchen game needs practice, while SNPickleball and Salt N Pepper Pickleball find soft shots easier with the bigger face. Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Nation describe a stiff or firm response, though Matt's Pickleball says it softens and gains dwell with use.

highlights.text: control the pop on midcourt resets

paras: Reviewers praise the strong spin, long dwell time and soft, muted feel, and see it suiting aggressive baseliners and players who want a longer handle for two handed backhands. Weight is the common complaint: swing weights of roughly 118 to 124 slow the hands in fast exchanges, as Matt's Pickleball, Pickleball Union and Pickleheads note, and Kev Knows Pickleball, Pickleheads and Johnkew Pickleball prefer the CRBN² TruFoam Genesis for stability, a bigger sweet spot or faster hands. Opinions on power vary, with Pickle Li and Paddle Addicts calling it a power paddle that is not top tier, Pickleheads finding strong power with extra pop, and Scooter Reviews Stuff saying it is not a pure power paddle.

highlights.text: slow the hands in fast exchanges

paras: Reviewers mostly recommend the standard-shaped second shape to players who want heavy spin, soft control and a foam core with no break-in or crushing. Power is where takes split: Johnkew Pickleball and Kev Knows Pickleball put it at the lower end, Matt's Pickleball in the middle, and STS PICKLEBALL leaning power, while Pickleball Studio says it is not a power paddle without added weight. WhiskyDink found less pop than the Joola Pro IV Scorpeus 16mm, and Tickle My Pickleball called the first session underwhelming before it grew on them.

highlights.text: not a power paddle without added weight

paras: Reviewers who like to shape the ball praise the exceptional spin, dwell and easy soft game, though several flag a high swing weight. Takes split on the sweet spot, which PickleTip calls large for a 14 mm paddle and Farmer Lanky Pickleball calls really good, while Pickleheads calls it small to medium and Johnkew Pickleball finds it narrow. Pickleball Willy found drives landed short until lead tape was added, and Pickleheads, Johnkew Pickleball and Kev Knows Pickleball prefer the CRBN² TruFoam Genesis.

Reviewers praise the dense, connected feel without a hollow echo, along with predictable power and good spin. Power placement varies: Pickleball Blast puts the elongated version at the lower to low mid end of the power category, while Matt's Pickleball measures it at the 89th percentile and says it matches the Loco on power. Forgiveness also splits by shape, with The Pickleball Dad calling the widebody sweet spot best in class, while The Sweet Spot Pickleball and Matt's Pickleball find the elongated less forgiving off center.

Reviewers praise it as an affordable foam paddle with high power and pop, suited to bangers and budget buyers, and several note it needs little added weight because of its internal weighting. Mixed takes come from the soft game and shape: Pickleball Studio and Pickleball On Call found resets and soft shots less consistent, while Pickleheads found control easy on the elongated but no elite pop. Reviewers including STS Pickleball and Pickleball Pursuit also point out that the grit does not last, so spin fades as the raw carbon face wears.

highlights.text: resets and soft shots less consistent

paras: Reviewers recommend it for aggressive, baseline driving players and budget buyers who want real power with a big sweet spot and plenty of spin, with Johnkew Pickleball and Famous by Friday Pickleball especially positive on the sweet spot. Mixed takes come from the soft game: Matt's Pickleball and Johnny Pickleball (PaddleCompare) found resets and blocks need adjustment so the ball stays low, while Famous by Friday Pickleball and Smash Pickleball found the plush dwell made control and defense easy. Spin durability is a repeated caution, with Johnkew Pickleball's lab test placing it in the lowest tier and Smash Pickleball expecting the grit to fade after roughly 10 to 20 hours.

highlights.text: real power with a big sweet spot

paras: Reviewers praise it as a high power hybrid with plenty of dwell, a large, stable sweet spot and fast hands at the net, and several, including Johnkew Pickleball, DDOG_Pickleball and Matt's Pickleball, prefer it to the elongated shape. Mixed takes come from the launch angle and soft game: Amir's Pickleball and Pickleball Studio found returns and resets harder to place, while Mid-Century Pickleball found resets incredible once the launch angle was set. All Drive No Drop Pickleball still preferred the elongated by a small margin, and several reviewers say the paddle suits players who can calibrate to a new, high powered paddle rather than beginners.

highlights.text: returns and resets harder to place

paras: Reviewers recommend it for aggressive players, baseline drivers and former tennis players, praising strong power, heavy topspin and fast hands, and several prefer the 16mm for softer, more controllable play over the 14mm, which pops more. Takes split on the sweet spot and soft game: Pickleball Union found a massive, forgiving sweet spot on the 16mm, while Mid-Century Pickleball and Martin Grunin Pickleball found it sits high and made slow dinks and soft resets harder. Pickleball Studio and Dink Kagè Pickleball found it more predictable than the Joola Perseus Pro IV, while Pickleball Studio and West Side Pickleball say durability is unproven, with core crush still possible.

highlights.text: slow dinks and soft resets harder

paras: Pickleheads and PickleTip call it a strong all-around paddle that blends power, control and forgiveness, and Paddle Addicts and Trung Active like its quick hands and touch at the kitchen. Opinions split on thickness: Pickleheads prefers the 16mm and finds the 14mm hard to control, while Mid-Century Pickleball found the 14mm sweet spot and stability better. West Side Pickleball finds it hard to recommend because of core crush worries and a face with almost no grit.

highlights.text: quick hands and touch at the kitchen
hard to recommend because of core crush

paras: Reviewers mostly suit it to players who want a softer, more controllable hybrid-shape paddle with mid-tier power, and the 16mm is preferred over the 14mm. JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Playbook liked it a lot, while most other reviewers called it a small step from the previous generation, with less pop, a smooth face and expected core crush. Pickleball Studio found the 14mm stiff with a small sweet spot, and Johnkew Pickleball called it probably overpriced for most players.

highlights.text: small step from the previous generation
stiff with a small sweet spot

paras: The Pickleball Wise, Pickleball Studio and Rylie's Review find it softer and a little more controlled than the Joola Perseus Pro IV, with dinks, drops and resets the best part while serves and drives feel much the same. Whether it is worth buying splits reviewers: Matt's Pickleball and Matthew K Pickleball call it a lateral or small step and point back to the Joola Perseus Pro IV, and Tickle My Pickleball finds the gain small next to its cost. Durability is unproven: Derik Hyndman Pickleball advises waiting after reports of paddles breaking, and Rylie's Review says a long term review is still needed.

highlights.text: softer and a little more controlled

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as an elongated Gen 3 power paddle with gritty spin, suited to aggressive intermediate and advanced players and former tennis players who want power on a budget. Opinions split on control and forgiveness: PickleBaller found a plush feel and generous sweet spot, while Pickle Li and vonEgypt Pickleball reported a smaller sweet spot and Pickleball Playbook found it lacks control. Against the Joola Perseus Pro IV, The New Main Pickleball and Womack Pickleball found power close to it with an easier or plusher feel, DY Pickleball found less pop, and sorrylee Pickleball names durability as the main flaw.

Reviewers mostly praise it as an elongated foam-core paddle with top-tier power, a large sweet spot and a hollow, muted feel, best for intermediate and advanced attackers, while beginners may find the pop too much. Soft-game takes split: Pickleball Playbook and Martin Grunin Pickleball found resets easy, while STS Pickleball and TIM Z struggled with drops and resets, and The New Main Pickleball found the muted feel gave little feedback on dinks and drops. Grit is the other sore point, as STS Pickleball, 패들러 and Martin Grunin Pickleball say the grit wears quickly, though Pickle Pick saw no spin drop-off after two weeks.

highlights.text: little feedback on dinks and drops

paras: Pickleheads, Pickleball Pursuit and Pickleball Studio praise the big pop, high spin and quick hands, and reviewers mostly recommend it to aggressive players who want a standard shape with a long handle. Thickness is the main split: Johnkew Pickleball and Pickleball Pursuit find the 12.7mm hits hardest but is harder to control, while the 14.3mm is the better choice for control. The soft game is the common warning, with Pickleball Effect saying resets and dinks need more skill and Pickleball Studio expecting the soft game to suffer.

highlights.text: big pop, high spin and quick hands
hits hardest but is harder to control
resets and dinks need more skill

paras: Pickleball Studio, Pickleball Pirates and Pickleball Effect praise the power, pop and spin and recommend the Gen 1 build to aggressive intermediate and advanced players. Reviewers split on thickness: Farmer Lanky Pickleball and Pickleball Studio find the 12.7mm poppier and harder to control, while JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Effect say the 14.3mm gives better touch and a more forgiving feel. The sweet spot is the common complaint, with KvPickleball, Briones Pickleball Breakdown and Daniel Pickleball reporting balls that die off the top, off center or on blocks.

highlights.text: praise the power, pop and spin
The sweet spot is the common complaint

paras: Pickleball Pursuit, All Drive No Drop Pickleball and STS PICKLEBALL praise the power and pop, and reviewers like the long 5.75 inch handle for two handed backhands. Cody Childers finds the 14.3mm softer and more controllable while the 12.7mm hits harder, and Benjamin Bramblett found the ball left the face too fast for loopy topspin thirds and resets in doubles. Reviewers find the sweet spot small, and Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Pursuit report a rattle from loose steel weights on 14.3mm units.

Reviewers praise the spin and fast hands, and Farmer Lanky Pickleball and JJ Pickleball both rate the sweet spot as top tier or amazing for an edgeless paddle, while Famous by Friday Pickleball calls it pretty good but not huge and says slow swingers will probably not get on with it. Mixed takes come from Hdbnb, who reports dead spots on the sides, and from SupaSenpai, who gave it a 1.0 over price and a bulge at the bottom of the head after a month, whereas JJ Pickleball says durability needs more time and Hdbnb found it holding up apart from edge damage. On price, Hdbnb would probably choose the CRBN TruFoam 2 at a similar cost, and Farmer Lanky Pickleball could only recommend it at a lower price, though that reviewer and JJ Pickleball both disclose Proton discount codes.

highlights.text: bulge at the bottom of the head

paras: Pickleball Playbook, Pickleheads and STS PICKLEBALL like the soft shots, quick hands and feel, with STS PICKLEBALL calling it the best feeling paddle they have hit. West Side Pickleball and JJ Pickleball say it benefits from added weight, and JJ Pickleball and Matt's Pickleball find the stock paddle stiff or unstable. Matt's Pickleball estimates the weighted paddle reaches about 95 percent of a comparison paddle's performance, while West Side Pickleball says the comparison paddle hits harder with less effort and has a far better sweet spot.

highlights.text: best feeling paddle they have hit

paras: Reviewers like the R4 hybrid for its quick hands and roomy handle, and say it becomes a real power paddle once weight is added at the sides or at 3 and 9 o'clock. Stock opinions are weaker, with WhiskyDink finding it flimsy and short on power and Pickleball Effect rating stock forgiveness below average. Matt's Pickleball found the weighted lineup close to another foam paddle for baseline pace, and Pickleball Effect found it still trailed that paddle slightly in power and pop.

Reviewers who liked the R4.14 praise its effortless power, sharp pop and quick hybrid shape, and it suits advanced players who can control that power. Matt's Pickleball and PickleTip both find the stock sweet spot tight or only average on forgiveness until tungsten or lead tape is added, while Pickleball Studio sees little room to add weight. JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Studio also describe a stiff, slightly tingy feel and less spin than earlier Ripples, and Johnkew Pickleball calls durability the big unknown for foam paddles.

Reviewers praise the spin and the soft, hollow feel, and the paddle suits players who value placement, resets and dinks over raw power, with Limitless Pickleball measuring it about 5 to 7 percent softer-hitting than the Q2. Mixed takes come mostly from grit durability and price: Pickleball Effect measured 96 percent of the grit roughness kept, while Johnkew Pickleball cited another tester's production units losing 350 to 400 RPM after about 50 games. Power ratings also disagree, with Pickleball Studio rating the 14 mm as low tier while JJ Pickleball found the 16 mm pop still high for touch shots.

highlights.text: pop still high for touch shots

paras: Reviewers mostly describe a light foam paddle that plays much like a Selkirk Boomstik, with big spin and power at a lower price, suited to aggressive players with a compact swing. Mixed takes center on the soft game and feel: Pickleheads and Pickleball Studio say resets take work, while Pickleball Playbook found soft shots easy to place, and Pickleball Willy reports an unpredictable hot spot near the center line. Grit durability also splits opinion, as The Sweet Spot Pickleball and Pickleball Studio say the texture wears quickly while Paddle Addicts saw no spin loss after about 10 hours.

highlights.text: plays much like a Selkirk Boomstik
unpredictable hot spot near the center line
no spin loss after about 10 hours

paras: Reviewers mostly describe a power-first paddle for experienced players, with strong pop and spin praised overall, including pop from Pickleball Studio and West Side Pickleball and spin from STS PICKLEBALL. Complaints about a small sweet spot and a board-like, jarring feel come up in most reviews, and several reviewers add lead or tungsten tape to help. Takes also split by version: Famous by Friday Pickleball, Coach Meredith Pollack and STS PICKLEBALL prefer the 10 mm, while Briones Pickleball Breakdown favors the Epic shape for control and Pickleheads liked the Epic's balance of pop and control.

Reviewers mostly praise the elongated Boomstik for top-end power and pop, a large sweet spot and easy spin, and it suits advanced players who want to attack. Mixed takes come from control: Pickleheads, STS PICKLEBALL and Rackets & Runners all note that the pop makes soft resets harder, and PaddleCompare finds it less forgiving in quick exchanges than the Selkirk LABS Project Boomstik Widebody. Matt's Pickleball and Pickleball Studio were the most mixed, citing loose or lifting edge guards, with Matt's Pickleball also questioning the value.

Reviewers praise the dense, foam-filled feel and a sweet spot better than most 14mm paddles, and it suits aggressive, attack-minded intermediate to advanced players. Takes split on the soft game: Pickleball Medicine heard one tester call it close to perfect, another call it too springy on dinks and resets, and a third ranked it last, while Pickleball Studio and All Drive No Drop Pickleball both said dinking needs some adjustment. Matt's Pickleball found the sweet spot smaller than on thicker paddles, Johnkew Pickleball said the sweet spot feels small, and Johnkew Pickleball passed on unverified Discord reports of quality problems.

highlights.text: too springy on dinks and resets
sweet spot smaller than on thicker paddles

paras: Reviewers mostly point to aggressive or power-leaning players who want elite spin and a forgiving sweet spot from a budget elongated paddle, with control that is easier than the power suggests. Takes split on pop and grit life: Pickleball Pursuit finds plenty of pop, while Matt's Pickleball reports muted pop on punch volleys, and Pickleball Effect recorded top abrasion retention while Pickleball Studio logged a 13 percent spin drop over 100 games. Farmer Lanky Pickleball advises players at 3.75 plus, and several reviewers add weight at 3 and 9 o'clock for more stability.

Reviewers mostly praise the extra pop, strong spin and value, and it suits players who want a stiff, hollow, ready-to-play paddle with power they can keep down. Grit durability is where takes split: Pickleball Studio measured spin falling about 29 percent on one unit after roughly five hours and Johnkew Pickleball recorded a tier one result by only a thin margin, while 50+Pickleball saw an almost new surface after over 10 hours. On control, Maiko and Pickleball Effect both found the Spartus Spitfire softer or easier to control, and Farmer Lanky warned players below 4.0 may struggle.

highlights.text: extra pop, strong spin and value

paras: Most reviewers like it as a plusher, more forgiving take on the original Power series, with good dwell for resets and drops. Several say it plays much like that cheaper paddle, so the higher price buys feel rather than performance. One mixed take calls it too much power for beginners, and the other would only buy it at a real discount.

highlights.text: plays much like that cheaper paddle

paras: Reviewers describe it as a high power Gearbox Gen 3 paddle for upper intermediate and advanced players, and Pickle Bill and Mid-Century Pickleball say it hits very hard and takes a session or several hours to get used to. Feel is where takes split: Pickleheads, Pickle Bill and Johnkew Pickleball found it stiff and hollow, while Pickleball Playbook Paddles found it plush and dwelling with very high control, and Jaysteel Dacudao praised precise drops and dinks. The Pickleball Pirates and Mid-Century Pickleball both note a very smooth face with little grit, and Tickle My Pickleball saw one crushed unit, so durability is still unproven.

highlights.text: a very smooth face with little grit

paras: Reviewers mostly like it as a stable all-court hybrid that handles dinks, drops and resets well, and several compare it with the Invader or the old Loco. Power is linear and not top of the market, so players wanting more should look elsewhere. The one mixed take finds it quick in the hand but says it does not carry players through resets.

highlights.text: does not carry players through resets

paras: Two of the three mixed takes call it a control paddle with a soft, dampened feel and limited pop, and one also finds low spin. The third finds thinner versions chaotic and prefers the 19 mm for consistency. WearTesters, the one positive review, instead finds strong pop on the elongated Pro 14 and likes its long handle.

Reviewers who like it, including Pickleball Effect, The Pickleball Pirates, Pickleball Tech Dude and Pickleball Blast, favor the hybrid for different reasons, including extra control and reach, a predictable full fiberglass face and long dwell time for shaping shots. Pickleball Studio, Farmer Lanky Pickleball and STS PICKLEBALL find the sweet spot small or worse than on the CRBN⁴ TruFoam Genesis, while Pickleball Effect notes dead spots near the top corners and Pickle Li uses added weight for forgiveness. Pickle Li and Pickleball Blast would main it over the CRBN⁴ TruFoam Genesis, while Farmer Lanky Pickleball would pick the CRBN² TruFoam Genesis or the CRBN⁴ TruFoam Genesis instead.

highlights.text: dead spots near the top corners

paras: Reviewers who like it point to more drive power than the CRBN¹ TruFoam Genesis, long dwell time and a soft, muted feel, and Pickleball Nation and Matt's Pickleball say the long handle helps two handed backhands. The main complaint is the sweet spot: Pickleball Studio and STS PICKLEBALL both say it drops off steeply and added weight helps little, Matt's Pickleball finds the edges drop off hard, and Pickleball Effect and West Side Pickleball note dead zones near the top or by the logo. Opinions on who it suits differ: STS PICKLEBALL calls it a sidegrade that suits few players, Pickleball Effect points it at higher level ball strikers who want reach, and West Side Pickleball picks it for maximum power once weight is added.

Reviewers say it suits advanced, aggressive power players who want strong pop and a dense, quiet feel, and Rackets & Runners and DDOG_Pickleball note it feels quick in the hand despite the high swing weight. Takes split on how hard it hits and how usable it is: STS Pickleball found power solid but no longer special and suggested the Gearbox GBX Power Elongated as a cheaper alternative with a much bigger sweet spot, while DDOG_Pickleball found it toned down and easier to reset than an older Gearbox power paddle, and Rackets & Runners called the power top tier. Several reviewers warn that the swing weight is already high so added weight is limited, and that the small sweet spot punishes off center hits.

highlights.text: strong pop and a dense, quiet feel

paras: Four reviewers praise the spin and a soft, dense or muted feel, with West Side and Pickleheads rating it high. Pickleball Playbook disagrees, finding at first that topspin drops rarely grab, with shots flying long or into the net. Power is modest, not a pure power paddle, and three reviewers say grit wear is unproven or unknown.

All three compare it with the Hyperion CFS 16, and two find it lighter and more controlled in the hand. Rackets & Runners and Pickleball Effect both say the grit wears faster, with Effect noting reduced grit after a couple of weeks. Famous by Friday, the one positive take, finds it forgiving and accurate but not a big spin paddle.

Reviewers mostly praise the very gritty face for heavy spin and dipping drives, and it suits spin-first players who want power and can handle a head-heavy swing. Mixed takes come from feel and control: Pickleball Studio Clips found a small, inconsistent sweet spot that needed added weight, while Pickleball Playbook Paddles called the sweet spot huge and stable. Pickle Li found resets unpredictable and Paddle Addicts found power lacking from the baseline, and several reviewers said grit durability is still unproven after limited play.

Reviewers who like it, such as Pickleball Adventure and vonEgypt Pickleball, praise the pop and controllable feel for a full foam paddle, and Pickleball Effect and JJ Pickleball find the face grittier than the Joola Perseus Pro V. Takes turn mixed on feel: Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Effect describe a stiff, hollow face with a small sweet spot, JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Advocate were not won over, and Famous by Friday Pickleball found it just okay. Grit durability is a recurring worry, and Not Dead Yet Pickleball preferred the RPM Jade for control and feel.

highlights.text: Grit durability is a recurring worry

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the pop, quick hands at the net and a sweet spot that several call large, and Tickle My Pickleball rates it among the best 14mm paddles. Mixed takes come from tape and control: Pickleball Medicine and The Pickleball Reviews found the stock sweet spot smaller than average until lead tape was added, and Daniel Pickleball, the only mixed review, found it stiff with random pop ups on drops and resets. Power is described differently too, as a power paddle all day by Matthew K Pickleball but more of an all court paddle by Pickleball Medicine.

highlights.text: stock sweet spot smaller than average
random pop ups on drops and resets

paras: Reviewers praise the very soft, plush feel and extra dwell, which suits players who want control on dinks, drops and resets and who can make their own power. Sweet spot opinions split: Pickleball Playbook Paddles and Pickleheads call it big and dependable, while Womack Pickleball finds it below average and Kev Knows Pickleball finds it small, and Matt's Pickleball and Kev Knows Pickleball both added weight to improve stability. Pickle Li and MyPickleList found distance hard to predict with more pop-up resets, and Pickleheads also found it head heavy and clunky.

highlights.text: control on dinks, drops and resets

paras: All three reviewers find strong power from a light paddle, with a swing weight near 100 at Pickleheads and Pickleball Studio. Pickleball Portal also finds hand speed and midcourt volleys quicker than a 16mm paddle. Portal finds the sweet spot small and Studio below average. They split on soft shots: Portal finds dinks, resets and drops controllable, while Studio finds resets frustrating at first. Pickleheads adds that the edgeless face dinged in the first session.

highlights.text: hand speed and midcourt volleys quicker

paras: All three reviewers call the power top tier or extraordinary. DDOG Pickleball finds the wide body forgiving, and JJ Pickleball rates the sweet spot the largest of any power paddle. DDOG and Matt's Pickleball both add lead or tungsten tape to the very light stock weight. Matt's finds the extra pop makes mishits pop up higher, and JJ worries the power ends points within three shots.

highlights.text: the sweet spot the largest of any power paddle

paras: Reviewers praise very high legal power and pop on drives, counters and overheads, and the paddle suits aggressive or advanced players who can handle a head-heavy elongated shape. Mixed takes from Pickleball Studio, Cody Childers, Rackets & Runners and Matt's Pickleball centre on a swing weight above 120, a tight sweet spot and slow hands in fast exchanges, and Pickleball Studio, Matt's Pickleball and Pickleball Medicine lean toward the Ronbus Ripple V2 R4.14 hybrid instead. Several reviewers also say spin is lower than the earlier beta version, and two reviewers call the durability of the foam core unknown.

Reviewers praise elite pop and power, with a big sweet spot on the widebody, and Pickleball Studio finds it plays almost like a Selkirk Boomstik. Control is the common trade: Pickleball Playbook says balls fly long once the swing extends, STS Pickleball calls control the catch, Pickleball Studio finds resets and drops the hardest part, and Pickle Li finds height harder to dial in. One TikTok creator likes the softer RPM Jade Widebody better for kitchen control.

highlights.text: balls fly long once the swing extends
resets and drops the hardest part

paras: Reviewers rate it highly for players who want power with forgiveness, and Ontario Pickleball Academy calls it well rounded enough for beginners and elite players alike. Power is where takes differ: Pickle Li calls it mid-tier and Matt's Pickleball says to skip it for maximum raw power without modification, while Ontario Pickleball Academy finds the power easy to deploy though below Boomstik level. Pickle Li also reports some grit variance between units and core crushing concerns, and Ontario Pickleball Academy finds it head heavy from stock.

Reviewers praise the fast hands at the net and the spin: STS PICKLEBALL recorded the highest spin among the low swing weight and edgeless paddles it compared, and Briones Pickleball Breakdown called control top tier. Power takes are split, with Farmer Lanky Pickleball finding very high pop but subpar power, Briones Pickleball Breakdown calling power nothing special, and BK Pickleball finding power exceptional. BK Pickleball also warned players with tennis elbow or wrist problems to stay away because of the low twist weight.

Reviewers like it as a denser, more controllable take on the Six Zero Black Opal 14mm, with Pickleball Effect measuring elite power and very high spin. Opinions split on how much power it has: West Side Pickleball places it among the most powerful approved paddles, while JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Blast place it in the mid tier, and Matthew K Pickleball finds less firepower than some players want. Pickle Li and MyPickleList found third shot drops floated, and Pickleball Blast and Pickleball Effect say the durability of the SharkSkin grit is unproven or likely to fade sooner than Diamond Tough.

highlights.text: elite power and very high spin

paras: Reviewers who liked it, including Pickleball Blast, Pickleball Pursuit and Salt N Pepper Pickleball, point to spin and shot shaping for intermediate to advanced players, while Pickleball Medicine, Matt's Pickleball and PickleTip describe a dense, connected feel. Mixed takes come mostly from the small sweet spot and a swing weight that Pickleball Blast and InfoTechYeti found high for a 14mm paddle, plus the question of added weight, which Matt's Pickleball and PickleTip say the elongated wants most, while Famous by Friday Pickleball advises against adding much. STS Pickleball and Matt's Pickleball were the least keen, with STS Pickleball preferring the Enhance MPP Turbo ArmorGrit and Matt's Pickleball wanting a poppier response.

Reviewers praise strong, predictable power and a big sweet spot at a budget price, with Pickleball Effect measuring Tier 1 grit durability. Touch is the trade: Matt's Pickleball finds resets sit up and drops run long, Pickleball Playbook says drops took extra effort, and four reviewers call the feel stiff or hollow. Pickleball Pursuit calls the grit not durable.

Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Studio Clips loved the high spin and forgiving sweet spot, while Matt's Pickleball was mixed. Power is where takes split: Matt's Pickleball found it too poppy in stock form, Pickleball Studio called it a poppy power paddle, and Pickleball Studio Clips called it low tier power out of the box. Matt's Pickleball picks the elongated for anyone undecided, and grit loss ranged from 8 to 10% after 30 hours to 13% after 100 games.

highlights.text: high spin and forgiving sweet spot
low tier power out of the box

paras: Pickleball Union recommends the 16mm version to intermediate to advanced players with a tennis background, and Pickleball Playbook calls it a great singles paddle with effortless depth from the baseline. Control is where takes split: Pickleball Playbook finds resets and defensive drops poor, with balls dumping into the net, while Pickleball Union rates control as one of the strongest parts. Dink n Drive, on the 14mm 2026 edition, likes the spin but says other paddles offer more value.

Reviewers mostly praise the spin from the licensed HexGrit surface, along with a soft, hollow feel that suits all-court play and touch at the kitchen. Opinions split on the sweet spot: Pickleball Pursuit and Austin Hardy call it large or huge, while SupaSenpai calls it small and STS Pickleball scores it about average for a hybrid. Many reviewers also found the stock weight light and added tape, and STS Pickleball found it less poppy than the Honolulu J2CR Blue Grit.

highlights.text: spin from the licensed HexGrit surface

paras: Reviewers praise its pop, spin and control for a power paddle, and The Pickleball Pirates and Matt's Pickleball both picked the 16mm over the 14mm. Mixed takes come from feel and price: Salt 'N Brine Picklers and West Side Pickleball found it stiffer or muted with a smaller sweet spot than the JOOLA Pro IV Hyperion, though West Side Pickleball still picked it for the extra grit, and SupaSenpai said the curved top shape puts off many players. Pickle Li, on YouTube and MyPickleList, rates it about level with the Engage Profoam, with more firepower but slightly less shot shaping.

Reviewers mostly praise a light, quick elongated paddle with strong pop and spin, with the 14mm more powerful and the 16mm softer and easier to control, as Pickleball Pursuit and Johnkew Pickleball describe. Pickleball Medicine and Matt's Pickleball found it needs added weight to feel stable, while JJ Pickleball and Johnkew Pickleball found it easier to play stock than the Franklin C45 Hybrid. Pickleball Union reported that the metallic edge guard scuffs easily, and Johnkew Pickleball saw matte edge guard paint wearing off.

highlights.text: needs added weight to feel stable

paras: Reviewers praise the Zen S+ for easy power at a swing weight around 107 and a very large sweet spot, and Pickleball Effect ranked it first for power in a group of MPP foam paddles. Opinions split on pop and spin: Pickleball Effect and Not Dead Yet Pickleball found pop low, Pickleball Playbook called spin average, and SupaSenpai said the production paddle shipped with less grit than early units, while Matthew K Pickleball found spin very good. Not Dead Yet Pickleball, the one mixed take, found a flat spot near the throat and would choose the 11SIX24 Ultre.

Reviewers praise the huge, forgiving sweet spot and control of the widebody, and recommend it for beginners and control-minded players on a budget. Power is the common limit: RYE3D Printing found many drives die before the back of the court, and STS Pickleball measured soft power and pop well below average. Takes differ on spin and wear, as Pickleheads called the spin strong for fiberglass and expects it to hold up, while STS Pickleball says the raw carbon face loses grit as it wears smooth.

highlights.text: many drives die before the back of the court
soft power and pop well below average

paras: Johnny K and Pickleball Playbook praise the widebody for controlled dinks, drops and resets, and Pickleball Playbook and Pickleball Studio credit it with a big sweet spot. Farmer Lanky Pickleball finds it overpriced and Pickleball Studio calls it a small update, while Pickleball Playbook favors it for most players below roughly the 5.0 level. Core crush is the shared worry: Derik Hyndman Pickleball relays early breakage reports and Pickleball Studio still sees a risk.

highlights.text: Core crush is the shared worry

paras: Reviewers praise the power, pop and a roomy sweet spot, with Cody Childers and Pickleball Medicine both loving it and Johnkew Pickleball picking it as the most forgiving of the three shapes. Takes turn mixed on weight and control: Pickleball Studio finds the sweet spot tight and the paddle slow for a widebody, All Drive No Drop thinks the sweet spot is about average, and Pickleball Tech Dude says resets are hard to soften. Three reviewers prefer the R4 hybrid over this shape, and Johnkew Pickleball notes that EVA foam durability is unproven.

Reviewers praise the Integra XL for a very quiet, dampened feel and a mix of forgiveness and maneuverability, with Matt's Pickleball, Briones Pickleball Breakdown and Pickleball Pursuit all liking it. Mixed takes come mostly from the sweet spot and the stock setup: Pickleball Studio rated the sweet spot subpar stock and Pickleball Medicine found it average to slightly small, while Briones called it huge. Pickleheads found it head-heavy and pricey, and named the Six Zero DBD Control as a better all-rounder for less.

Most reviewers praise the control, spin and large sweet spot of this light hybrid, with resets, drops and dinks drawing the most positive comments. Mixed takes come from power and feel: Mid-Century Pickleball found a longer break-in and less dwell time than the Luzz Glider 2024, and Pickleball Willy found it stiffer with harder drops and dinks, while Pickleheads called the pop explosive, though most reviewers who compared it with the Luzz Cannon found the Cannon hits harder. Grit life is the other open question, with The New Main Pickleball seeing wear near the center after about 10 hours and Spinwave Pickleball reporting the grit wore off after the first day.

highlights.text: control, spin and large sweet spot
longer break-in and less dwell time
wear near the center after about 10 hours

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the quiet sound with strong power and pop, and Famous by Friday Pickleball and Pickleball Portal both say the soft foam face suits sore arms. Takes split on control: Kev Knows Pickleball and To Pickleball & Beyond found it hard to dial back, while Famous by Friday Pickleball and Pickleball Portal describe a trampoline feel that settles once the swing is calibrated, and Pickleball Union reports control coming together by the second and third games. To Pickleball & Beyond and Famous by Friday Pickleball also both compare it with the Diadem Vice and see the Hush as the more controllable of the two.

highlights.text: quiet sound with strong power and pop

paras: Reviewers who liked it point to more control and a bigger sweet spot than the Pro Power, with Pickleball Portal and JJ Pickleball the most positive. Mixed takes come from weight: Pickleball Effect, Matthew K Pickleball and Johnkew Pickleball all call it heavy, head heavy or sluggish in stock form, and Matthew K prefers the original Pro Power Elongated for its fast hands at the kitchen. Pickleball Effect and Johnkew Pickleball added tungsten tape, which lowered the balance point and left it feeling more stable or no heavier.

highlights.text: more control and a bigger sweet spot

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the Quartz for soft-game control, a plush feel and a light swing weight, and several suggest it for beginners or a first upgrade. Sweet spot size is where takes split: BK Pickleball and The Pickleball Pirates call it huge, while STS Pickleball calls it very tight and Pickleheads finds it small for a square shape. STS Pickleball also recommends the Six Zero Ruby or Double Black Diamond over it, and reviewers agree power is low, with several mentioning lead tape as an adjustment.

Reviewers praise the power and spin of this fiberglass faced hybrid, and Pickleball Pirates and Famous by Friday Pickleball also found a large sweet spot. Takes split on control: Pickleheads, Tickle My Pickleball and Pickleball Effect found the stiff feel made drops and resets harder, while Famous by Friday Pickleball found accuracy and control excellent. Pickleheads, Pickleball Will and Pickleball Pirates each point to the Six Zero Double Black Diamond Control as the safer choice for most players, or for doubles.

Reviewers mostly praise the hybrid shape for its low swing weight, quick hands at the net and strong spin, with Pickleball Blast and Matt's Pickleball both measuring swing weights around 107. Mixed takes come from price and from players already on an earlier shape: Pickleball Studio calls the Honolulu J2NF the better paddle overall, and Pickleball Tech Dude doubts it is worth trying for players who already own a one through three shape. Several reviewers also add tungsten or lead tape because the stock sweet spot is smaller than some rivals.

Reviewers mostly describe an aggressive spin and power paddle, with Pickleheads rating the spin among the best they have tested. Takes split on the sweet spot and power: PickleTip found a large, forgiving sweet spot, while Pickleball Effect found a small sweet spot and less power than the Paddletek Bantam and JOOLA Pro IV. Several reviewers also found the head-heavy balance slow at the net and preferred the thinner 12.7mm there.

highlights.text: head-heavy balance slow at the net

paras: Reviewers praise the Perseus 3S Dual for control and a stable feel, with The Raw Reviews recommending the 16mm version to intermediate to advanced players who want reach and a premium feel, and vonEgypt Pickleball seeing the 14mm as a cheaper, easier alternative to the Pro 4. Takes differ on power: Dink n Drive found somewhat less power than the original Perseus 3S and called slice spin only okay, while vonEgypt Pickleball noted a slight drop in power and pop against the Pro 4. Dink n Drive saw no crushed core after roughly 150 to 200 hours, though one Reddit player reported a cracking noise from the core after around three months.

Reviewers praise the soft, dense feel and the extra pop of the 16mm widebody, with Matt's Pickleball finding the sweet spot big and consistent and Johnkew Pickleball calling the R2 the safest pick for most players. Takes split on forgiveness, as Pickleball Effect measured a 6.62 twist weight against a 7.25 widebody average and struggled to control it, while Spinwave Pickleball rated the sweet spot slightly above average for the shape. Matt's Pickleball also reported that their R2 delaminated after hours of drilling in 90 to 95 degree heat, though the other three shapes held up.

Reviewers praise the spin and the soft, dense feel that makes resets, drops and dinks easy, and it suits players who bring their own pace. Opinions split on stability: Pickleball Playbook found it top heavy with the sweet spot far from the hand, and MyPickleList found a smaller sweet spot in stock form but more stability with 3 g added at 3 and 9 o'clock, while Matt's Pickleball called the sweet spot large. Several reviewers prefer the Ultre, though Pickleball Effect picked the Vapor over it.

Reviewers praise the Hybrid-W as a quick, stable paddle with easy blocks and resets, with Pickleball Effect measuring a 107 swing weight and The Pickleball Reviews 107.4. Most comparisons are against the Pakle Fuse Elongated, which reviewers describe as having more power and reach, while PaddleCompare (Johnny Pickleball) found the Hybrid-W better for control and resets, though from separate sessions rather than head-to-head play. Grit durability draws the most caution: Pickleball Effect rated it top, but Matthew K Pickleball and The Pickleball Reviews both mention earlier batches with problems and say the latest needs more time.

Reviewers mostly praise the pop and pace, along with a sweet spot that several call large for an elongated shape, and Pickleball Willy, Pickleball Playbook Paddles, SNPickleball and Spinwave Pickleball all loved it. The mixed takes come from the soft game: Nico the Lefty said it punishes drops and resets, STS Pickleball said dinks float, and Spinwave Pickleball expects a short adjustment period for players coming from control paddles. Against the Cyclone Hybrid, Pickleball Willy and Nico the Lefty found the elongated more powerful, while WhiskyDink found the two play much alike.

highlights.text: sweet spot that several call large

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the 13mm elongated Halo Power for extra pop over the 16mm Control XL with little control lost, and three call the sweet spot large or massive. Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Effect are the mixed voices, with Pickleball Studio finding resets at the kitchen harder and balls sitting up, and adding lead tape for stability, a step that several other reviewers also mention. Spin readings of 1400 to 1450 RPM from Pickleball Portal and Pickleballogist fall below other raw carbon paddles that reach 1600 RPM.

highlights.text: extra pop over the 16mm Control XL
fall below other raw carbon paddles

paras: The hybrid Barrage 4 suits players who want fast hands, spin and put-away power, and West Side Pickleball, The Honest Take and Pickleheads all liked it, though several reviewers added weight to settle it. Takes split on the sweet spot and pop: West Side Pickleball calls the sweet spot the best of any 14mm they have played, while MyPickleList finds it below average to average in stock form and rates power as mid-tier. Reviewers who also played the standard Barrage 2 call it the more forgiving shape, with the 4 being the spicier one.

highlights.text: fast hands, spin and put-away power
below average to average in stock form

paras: Reviewers who liked it point to spin and controlled power for aggressive players who can hit the center, with the 2 and 4 shapes picked most often. Takes split on power: Pickleheads put it near the top of the market, while Farmer Lanky Pickleball placed it at the bottom of the power category and Pickleball Tech Dude found the gain over the Genesis too small. Every reviewer criticizes the small sweet spot, and several also object to the price.

Reviewers mostly like it for a very wide, forgiving sweet spot and a light, maneuverable feel, with power that stays controllable. Takes differ on power: RYE3D Printing found it the most powerful of the Power paddles on drives, while Johnkew Pickleball and Pickleball Tech Dude found it the least powerful of the three shapes but the poppiest. Pickleball Studio and RYE3D Printing both said the pop takes adjusting on resets and at the net, and PickleTip, the one mixed review, found the original 16mm version firmer and worth buying only at a clear discount.

Reviewers praise the soft, dense feel and the spin and control it gives for resets, drops and dinks, and it suits players who generate their own pace. Mixed takes come mostly from power and weight: Pickleball Playbook picks it as the paddle they trust most in a tournament, while West Side Pickleball found a flat sound and heavier feel and would pay for the Power 2 instead. Pickleball Effect and STS Pickleball both note a heavy swing weight that slows hands at the kitchen, and each lists it as UPA-A approved but not USA Pickleball approved.

Reviewers who liked it point to strong power from an elongated shape that does not feel sluggish, with Pickleball Effect and Johnkew Pickleball both playing it without added weight. Mixed takes come from the sweet spot: Matthew K Pickleball found it bigger than the Vapor's, while Pickleball Effect, STS PICKLEBALL and PickleTip found it tighter or narrower. Johnkew Pickleball and STS PICKLEBALL both preferred the Vapor, and Pickleball Tech Dude rated this the most powerful but least poppy of the three.

highlights.text: strong power from an elongated shape

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the widebody Shift for quick hands, strong spin and a forgiving sweet spot, and it suits players who want control with moderate power. Matt's Pickleball gave the mixed take, finding the feel too dense and muted for their taste, and STS Pickleball also called it denser than the plush feel others report. Power comparisons vary: Farmer Lanky Pickleball places it between the Honolulu NF series and the Loco, while Pickleheads says the Loco offers more power out of the box.

Reviewers praise the spin and power and report a damped, low vibration feel, with Matt's Pickleball preferring it to the Diadem Warrior BluCore and West Side Pickleball calling the 16 mm an upgrade over the Diadem Edge 18K Power Pro. The Pickleball Pirates and Famous by Friday Pickleball find the 16 mm plush and forgiving, while Tickle My Pickleball and Matt's Pickleball report a stiff feel, with Matt's Pickleball finding a stiff, jarring feel on mishits and West Side Pickleball noting a dead spot off center on the 16 mm. Pickleball Addict Life and SupaSenpai say soft shots are less forgiving or take time to learn, and Matt's Pickleball and Famous by Friday Pickleball find weaker value than other foam paddles.

Reviewers praise the plush, soft feel and spin, and it suits players who want touch with a little more power than the original LUXX. Johnkew Pickleball and Pickleball Effect measured a low stock twist weight (5.9 and 5.83), and Pickleball Nation found the narrower face less forgiving, while West Side Pickleball rated the sweet spot as very generous. Pickleball Effect called the price hard to justify, whereas West Side Pickleball thought it probably warranted.

Reviewers who liked it were mostly after spin and control, with Rackets & Runners and All Drive No Drop pointing to Kevlar plushness and soft touch, and Pickleball Medicine noting a consistent face feel. Takes on power split against the Mach Forza: Pickleball Medicine and Farmer Lanky found slightly more pop and power than the Mach 1 Forza, while The Pickleball Pirates found less power and spin than the Mach line, and All Drive No Drop found power and pop lacking. Control is also mixed, as Rackets & Runners found it better for control but less consistent than the Mach 1 Forza, and Farmer Lanky found it harder to handle.

Reviewers broadly praise it as a well-rounded power paddle, with Pickleball Pursuit and All Drive No Drop calling it the best Selkirk by a wide margin and Famous by Friday singling out spin and dwell time. Mixed takes come from shape and power level: Pickleball Willy calls the widebody very forgiving but capped around six or seven out of ten power, while Pickleheads finds the elongated sweet spot noticeably tight and Johnkew Pickleball finds it generous. Against the 11SIX24 Hurache-X Power, Pickleball Tech Dude finds the ERA Power more responsive, while Pickleball Effect says the 11SIX24 Power is nearly as good for less, and several reviewers note durability is unproven.

highlights.text: best Selkirk by a wide margin

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the 16mm for a soft feel, easy control on resets and drops, and a quicker swing than the Hyperion, with Rackets & Runners calling it the softest and most controlled thermoformed paddle it tried. Takes split on price and power: The Pickleball Pirates call it a good buy while Farmer Lanky Pickleball would not recommend it at that price, and Derik Hyndman finds more pop than the Hyperion while Pickleball Effect and Rackets & Runners find less power than other thermoformed paddles. Famous by Friday Pickleball, STS Pickleball and Briones Pickleball Academy all point to a smaller sweet spot that hurts on off-center hits.

highlights.text: softest and most controlled thermoformed paddle
would not recommend it at that price

paras: Reviewers mostly praise a dense, plush feel, a large sweet spot and easy all-court control across the X, S and V shapes. Comparisons with the Pulse split on pop: Womack Pickleball and Tickle My Pickleball found slightly more pop, while DDOG_Pickleball found the Pulse hotter and the Harmony more controllable. Mixed takes come from price and power, with Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Effect questioning the price against cheaper rivals, and vonEgypt Pickleball finding baseline power short in about three hours of play.

Reviewers mostly suit it to players who liked the original Loco and want the same stiff, hollow feel with more spin and grit that lasts, and Pickleball Studio measured spin holding through 117 games. Mixed takes come from control, as STS Pickleball leans toward the Hybrid for most players because the Elongated has a smaller sweet spot, and PickleTip picks the Hybrid by a small margin because the Elongated is less forgiving off-center. Axel Lee Pickleball and Johnkew Pickleball both warn that the springy pop makes midcourt resets hard, and Johnkew ran their grit wear test on a Hybrid only.

highlights.text: more spin and grit that lasts
springy pop makes midcourt resets hard

paras: Reviewers praise the Holbrook Arma T for big pop, spin and a roomy sweet spot for a 14mm paddle, and it suits aggressive drivers who can handle a high swing weight. Mixed takes come mainly from durability, where Johnkew Pickleball, Pickleball Pursuit and Pickleball Studio cited core crush in a cut open unit or X-rays and advised waiting, and from feel, where Paddle Addicts reported jarring off-center hits while vonEgypt Pickleball found none. Pickleball Portal and Famous by Friday Pickleball, who used the metallic version, saw no play loss yet but both noted occasional flyers and said it is not for control-first players.

highlights.text: big pop, spin and a roomy sweet spot

paras: Reviewers including Johnkew Pickleball, STS PICKLEBALL and All Drive No Drop Pickleball praise the large sweet spot, good spin and stable power for a hybrid power paddle. Mixed takes come from drives and the soft game: District Pickleball and RYE3D Printing found drives hard to dial in stock until weight was added, while Pickleball Studio called the soft game not a strength. WhiskyDink and Pickleball Pursuit both put it a step below the Joola Scorpeus Pro IV 16mm, with less power and pop.

Reviewers mostly praise the Hybrid for control, a consistent sweet spot and spin from the 18K carbon face, and MyPickleList says it works in stock form without mods. Feel is where takes split: Tickle My Pickleball finds it the stiffest of any Gen 4 paddles and Pickle Li and MyPickleList call it firm, while The Pickleball Pirates describe a plush face with a wide sweet spot. Power also varies, with Tickle My Pickleball rating pop high, especially on the 14mm, while Pickle Li, MyPickleList and Pickleball Portal place it below paddles such as the RPM or Boomstik.

highlights.text: below paddles such as the RPM or Boomstik

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as a power widebody with a big, stable face, and it suits players who like widebody shapes and want power with control. Takes differ on how much power it has: All Drive No Drop rates top-end power among the best in the game, while PickyPaddle says it is not a power paddle and that a short swing lands short. Paddle Addicts and Francis Rances were mixed, citing a stiffer feel and less drive power in one case and a very poppy 14mm that is too powerful for touch players in the other.

Reviewers praise the spin, reach and power of the elongated V2, with Pickleheads calling it the best spin of any paddle right now and Ontario Pickleball Academy picking it for players who want more reach. Takes split on feel and comfort: Pickleball Studio and vonEgypt Pickleball like the stiff, hollow response, while PB HEAT found the square stock handle painful and Famous by Friday Pickleball found a sweet spot a touch smaller than the earlier version. Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Willy both warn that the paddle can core crush.

highlights.text: best spin of any paddle right now

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the power and a very large sweet spot, which suits attackers more than soft game players, and several reviewers warn that the pop makes soft shots harder to control. Opinions split on value and spin: Matt's Pickleball cannot recommend it at that price because similar performance costs less, while Pickleball Effect measured below-average spin at 1,980 RPM against about 2,300 from Johnkew Pickleball and STS Pickleball. Edge guard loosening or lifting comes up in several reviews, though some cases involved the elongated shape or removed weights.

highlights.text: makes soft shots harder to control

paras: Reviewers who like it point to the quick hand speed, and Matthew K Pickleball picked the 14mm as the most well-rounded for pop, feel and spin. Pickleball Studio and Matt's Pickleball both found the sweet spot small in stock form, especially on the 12.7mm, and all four reviewers either added weight or said it needs it. SupaSenpai, on a 16mm demo with no weight allowed, found less control than the original C45 and called it too expensive.

highlights.text: sweet spot small in stock form

paras: Reviewers praise a big sweet spot, forgiving feel and quick hands in hands battles, and Johnkew Pickleball measured a KewCOR of 0.416, well above the Honolulu J3NF. Takes are mixed on control and balance: Pickleball Playbook found it more jarring on off-center hits and top heavy, and still picked the Honolulu J2CR, while Wongsquared found fast dinks harder to control and would now lean toward the Honolulu J6CR. Grit durability is split, with Not Dead Yet rating the Crystal Blue Endurance surface tier one while West Side Pickleball said the paddle lacks a durable grit surface.

Reviewers mostly praise the soft, plush feel, the large sweet spot and the control on dinks, drops and resets, with several recommending it for all court play. Takes split on spin and pop: Scooter Reviews Stuff rates spin as top tier and Pickleheads calls it elite, while STS Pickleball found less grip on rolls, Daniel Pickleball calls spin good but not amazing, and Farmer Lanky Pickleball puts pop in the lower tier. STS Pickleball and Pickleheads gave the two mixed ratings, citing a harder drop off outside the sweet spot and a heavy, slow feel at the net.

Reviewers praise the EPP Turbo as a budget power paddle with a large sweet spot, and Pickleball Playbook and Austin Hardy both say frame hits and shanks still go in. Mixed takes come from comparisons: STS Pickleball and The Pickleball Reviews both prefer the MPP Turbo, while Pickleball Tech Dude and Pickleball Studio Clips each put it at about 90% of the Bread & Butter Loco for far less money. Opinions on the hybrid shape split, with All Drive No Drop saying its smaller face hurts returns and resets, while Pickleball Tech Dude preferred it to the Bread & Butter Loco Hybrid hybrid.

highlights.text: smaller face hurts returns and resets

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the soft, plush feel and long dwell time, which make dinks, drops and resets easy, with power described as all-court or lower-end rather than explosive. Takes split on shape: the elongated X has a swing weight of roughly 121 to 124 that Tickle My Pickleball, Johnkew Pickleball and TIM Z point to as heavy, while DDOG_Pickleball and Pickleball Medicine pick the V widebody as a favorite and Matt's Pickleball says the V never came together. Sweet spot ratings range from large (Famous by Friday Pickleball) to solid but not best in class (Johnkew Pickleball).

Reviewers such as PickleBaller and Pickleball Playbook Paddles praise the easier control on drops and resets, and it suits players who found the Selkirk Boomstick too hot but still want power. Takes turn mixed on how much is given up: most say power and pop sit below the Boomstick, while JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Studio found it stiff and poppy with the weights on and softer only with them off. Grit durability and price drew complaints from Nico the Lefty, while JJ Pickleball also doubted the grit, and Pickleheads called it hard to justify.

highlights.text: easier control on drops and resets

paras: Reviewers who like power praise the big pop, large sweet spot and light, fast swing for an elongated shape, and most point it at advanced or offense-first players with soft hands. Opinions split on grit durability: Pickleball Effect saw it hold 96% in durability testing, while Pickleball Tech Dude measured spin retention of 88% after 10,000 shots and Maiko noted slight spin loss. Pickleball Review found the Spartus Spitfire softer and easier for drops, and Pickleball Pursuit found resets tricky because of the boingy pop.

Reviewers mostly praise it as the same feel as the Bread & Butter Loco with a grittier face that adds spin and has held up so far, along with a roomy sweet spot and quick hands. Mixed takes come from the lively pop, with From Tennis to Pickleball finding soft shots too poppy and STS Pickleball rating control below average for a hybrid, while Matthew K Pickleball found it stiffer and more predictable than the original. On comparisons, Pickleball Playbook Paddles rated it slightly ahead of the 11SIX24 Ultré Power 2, while STS Pickleball called the two about even.

highlights.text: a grittier face that adds spin
control below average for a hybrid

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the huge sweet spot, strong spin and easy control, and suggest it for players wanting a forgiving all-court foam paddle. Power is where takes split: All Drive No Drop Pickleball rated serves and drives among the best they have had, while West Side Pickleball found it less powerful than the Bread & Butter Loco, and Pickleball Studio did not put it on par with the hardest hitters. Several reviewers describe it as firmer and poppier than the Honolulu J2FC+ and the Honolulu J2NFT, and Pickleball Medicine and SupaSenpai both flagged the short handle as a problem for backhands.

highlights.text: less powerful than the Bread & Butter Loco

paras: Reviewers mostly praise a soft, plush feel that makes dinks, drops and resets easy, along with good spin and a low swing weight. In head-to-heads with the Honolulu J2NF, UnforcedErrorsPB, The Sweet Spot Pickleball and STS PICKLEBALL found it more control oriented and a little less powerful, while Matthew K Pickleball found it poppier and prone to popping soft hits up. The handle drew complaints too, with Pickleball Medicine saying it does not allow two hands and Pickleball Studio saying it plays closer to 5.25 inches.

Reviewers who prefer the Gearbox Pressure X 8E over its stiffer sibling praise its softer, more hollow feel, longer dwell and a big, predictable sweet spot, and suggest it for players who want touch at the kitchen. Takes split on power and value: Pickleball Playbook found it more poppy than powerful, Matt's Pickleball and Womack Pickleball placed power mid range, Farmer Lanky Pickleball put it at the top of the category, Not Dead Yet Pickleball picked the Honolulu J6CR M105 over it, and Womack Pickleball found it hard to recommend on value. Grit gets mixed reports too, with Pickleball Tech Dude finding over 90% of spin retained after a 10,000 shot test, while Matt's Pickleball called the grit not durable and Johnkew Pickleball found the face smooth.

Reviewers who like a stiff, hollow power paddle mostly praise the extra spin over the original Selkirk Boomstik, and several also like the removable MOI weights. Opinions split on grit life: Pickleball Studio measured about 25% less surface roughness after roughly 37 games and could not recommend its unit, while STS PICKLEBALL found the grit holding up fairly well with its test under halfway done. Power and control also vary, with some reviewers finding it slightly less powerful and easier to manage than the original and others finding it equally strong, and several call it pricey.

Reviewers mostly praise it as a J2Ti with more power, big spin and a large sweet spot, and it suits players who want Gen 3 pop without giving up a soft feel. Mixed takes come from the control trade-off: To Pickleball & Beyond calls it a slight loss against the J2Ti, while Wongsquared ranks it third of four and says kitchen control suffers, and All Drive No Drop Pickleball sees only a small change from the J2Ti. Durability is the other open question, since Gen 3 foam cores are expected to compress and some reviewers have not tested it long term.

highlights.text: big spin and a large sweet spot
Gen 3 foam cores are expected to compress

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the large, consistent sweet spot, a plush or muted foam feel and a gritty face that helps spin, with Famous by Friday Pickleball and Britt's Life in the Philippines among the most positive. Power is where takes split: CarpeDink'em Pickleball and John Wilkerson put it at the low end of the power range, Farmer Lanky Pickleball places it mid-level, and MyPickleList calls it a high-tier power paddle. Touch is the other split, as Amir's Pickleball found the muted feel gave no feedback and called it the worst paddle they have tested, while TGu needed added weight to steady return of serve.

Reviewers mostly praise strong power at a light swing weight, with a large sweet spot, and it suits aggressive intermediate to advanced players who swing through the ball. Takes split on the soft game and spin: Spinwave Pickleball and JJ Pickleball found low pop at slow speeds and resets that needed work, while EZY3D LAB found dinks, drops and resets controlled, and Pickleball Studio Clips measured spin well below many paddles while Famous by Friday Pickleball rated it very good. Not Dead Yet Pickleball, after about three games, found less pop and a flat spot near the throat, and would pick the 11SIX24 Ultre.

highlights.text: strong power at a light swing weight
a flat spot near the throat

paras: Reviewers recommend it for players who win with a soft game and want control on drops, dinks and resets more than put-away power. Mixed takes mostly come from power, where West Side Pickleball and All Drive No Drop Pickleball rank it behind the J6CR and J6 M+, and Matt's Pickleball got no power stock until adding side weight. Feel is another split, as Johnkew Pickleball's video and newsletter describe it as stiff and dense, while several other reviewers call it soft.

highlights.text: behind the J6CR and J6 M+

paras: Reviewers mostly describe it as a spin-heavy, powerful 14mm paddle for players who like a stiff, hollow, feedback-heavy feel, with Pickleball Playbook Paddles calling it the most control oriented 14mm they have played. Takes split on weight and stability by shape: Pickleball Tech Dude finds every shape heavy with little room for added weight, while Matt's Pickleball calls the hybrid light in stock form and adds a 3 g strip. Grit durability is a doubt for Pickleball Pursuit, West Side Pickleball and Nico the Lefty, and Farmer Lanky Pickleball suggests casual 3.5 players stay clear.

highlights.text: heavy with little room for added weight

paras: Royal Pickleball and Nate Nalven both liked it for top tier spin and controllable power, finding it easier to manage than the RPM Q2, while Matt's Pickleball found drives and drops going where aimed. Takes split on power and feel: RALLYHAUS called power low-tier with a hot spot that sent balls long and reported arm fatigue, and Famous by Friday found it consistent but with no standout trait, while Royal Pickleball and Nate Nalven said it feels weighty enough to need a choke up. Price is the other sticking point, and RALLYHAUS and Matt's Pickleball both noted there is no durable grit.

highlights.text: top tier spin and controllable power
drives and drops going where aimed
hot spot that sent balls long

paras: Reviewers mostly recommend it to J2K players who want more power while keeping the J2 shape's control, with a big sweet spot and gritty spin praised often. How much extra power it adds is disputed: DY Pickleball and Matthew K Pickleball found a clear gain, while Pickleball Effect rated power nearly identical to the J2K with less pop. Durability is the other split, since Pickle Techie reported core crush after over a month while DY Pickleball heard none after two months.

highlights.text: core crush after over a month

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the pop, spin and power of this Gen 1 hybrid shape, especially on the 12.7mm, and it suits aggressive players who can tame it. Power ratings differ, with Johnkew Pickleball placing the 12.7mm in the elite tier while Pickle Li and Paddle Addicts called it mid-tier. Sweet spot takes also split, as Pickleball Pursuit found it better than expected while Pickleball Studio called it tight, and several reviewers point to the 14.3mm as the easier option.

Reviewers mostly praise a big sweet spot and real power at a swing weight between about 110 and 115, with several calling the price fair.
