Opinions split on control and grit: Pickleball Rx called control amazing for resets, while SupaSenpai found it poppy at the kitchen and Matt's Pickleball struggled with resets and saw the grit wear quickly. Dr. Christy Price saw little grit change after a few weeks, and Mid-Century Pickleball and The Sweet Spot Pickleball could not yet confirm durability.

Reviewers mostly praise the spin and the crisp, stiff Gen 3 feel, with The Volley Zone and Royal Pickleball the most positive. Sweet spot reports split: Famous by Friday Pickleball calls the sweet spot small and says performance drops when contact wanders, while Royal Pickleball calls it large for an elongated shape and JJ Pickleball credits the full floating core for forgiveness on mishits. Power also varies, as All Drive No Drop Pickleball calls it one of the hardest hitting Gen 3 paddles while JJ Pickleball and The Volley Zone say others hit harder, and reviewers who ran it light often suggest adding weight.

Reviewers praise the soft, forgiving foam feel and stable sweet spot, with WIRED recommending it to beginners and Pickleball Effect to players who value touch and consistency over power. Takes turn mixed on baseline drives, dead spots and price: JJ Pickleball found the face muted on drives, Pickleball Medicine hit dead spots toward the edges and gave it a hard pass at that price, and Famous by Friday rated power and control as average. Comparisons to the Boomstik are common, and West Side Pickleball and Tickle My Pickleball both describe it as a softer, different paddle rather than a budget Boomstik.

Most reviewers liked the elongated Pop N Treasure for its pop, power and gritty spin, and Pickleball Rx and Pickleball Willy were the most positive about the power. Takes split on the soft game and spin: Pickleball Playbook found edges and corners dead and preferred the widebody, while Pickleball Rx rated spin only fair because the stiff build gives little dwell time. Pulpconnection found pop and power no better than other paddles and said the price is hard to judge against cheaper options, and some reviewers noted the Evergrit surface has not yet shown how long it lasts.

Reviewers mostly praise strong pop, a large forgiving sweet spot and a low swing weight that keeps it quick in hand, and two reviewers suggest it as a first power paddle rather than a beginner paddle. Power ratings vary: Pickleball Pursuit calls firepower almost elite, while Tickle My Pickleball found it the lowest of the hybrids tested, a step below the Spartus P1. The mixed takes from West Side Pickleball and Pickleball Studio centre on a thick handle, less spin than the Spartus P1 and difficulty controlling it for low power or all-court players.

Reviewers mostly praise a quick, maneuverable paddle with a large sweet spot and plenty of pop, and some measured swing weights between 108 and 110. Mixed takes come from sibling comparisons: Tickle My Pickleball found it gives up some reach and firepower compared with the original J2NF, and Pickleball Medicine ranked it second of three new shapes and fourth overall behind the J2 FC+, J2NF and J7NF. Power is also described differently, as ThomasFL put it at roughly 85% of the Loco while Matthew K Pickleball called it a bazooka.

highlights.text: gives up some reach and firepower

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the control, touch and low price, with Pickleheads calling it the best control and touch paddle they have used after 35 hours. Power is where takes split: Ethan Linder found hard hits did not travel far and would not recommend it to higher level players, while Matt's Pickleball logged above average power from a softer face with less snap than carbon fiberglass builds. Tournament eligibility is also reported differently, as The Paddle TestHers said it is UPA approved while Cody Childers said it is PPA approved but not USAPA, so check the rules before entering events.

highlights.text: hard hits did not travel far

paras: Reviewers praise the J2NFT for a soft, plush feel and a large sweet spot, and it suits players who want touch and control with some power. Mixed takes come from comparisons with the carbon J2 NF, which Matt's Pickleball and Pickleball Studio preferred, with Pickleball Studio saying the NFT offers nothing the J2NF or J2FC+ cannot. Matt's Pickleball also said the muted feel may be too much for players coming from bouncier paddles, while STS PICKLEBALL named the NFT a top pick alongside the NF.

highlights.text: offers nothing the J2NF or J2FC+ cannot
muted feel may be too much

paras: Reviewers who like it point to a generous sweet spot and control, with Pickleball Advocate finding it light and easy to swing from the first hits and Pickleball Rx rating spin as probably the best in its comparison group. Power is where takes split: SupaSenpai found drives and smashes the strongest, and a co-host on Matthew K Pickleball called the Gen 3 a top tier power paddle, while Pickleball Rx put power around seven out of 10 on the elongated 16mm and Pickleball Pontevedra found it short of finishing power next to the X5. Price and handle draw the most complaints, with four reviewers questioning the price and three flagging the handle shape as blocky, square or slightly rectangular, though Pickleball Advocate called it worth the money.

Reviewers praise it as a very light, quick elongated paddle for players who want hand speed and are happy to tune it with added weight. Mixed takes come from stock stability and power: JJ Pickleball found it unsteady on blocks until about three grams at 3 and 9 o'clock raised the swing weight to 115, while Matt's Pickleball named the Neonic Frost FLX as the steadier, more forgiving pick for most players. Spin is a second complaint, as Farmer Lanky Pickleball and Matt's Pickleball both say it has no durable grit.

Reviewers mostly praise a large sweet spot, drives that dip low with real power, and a soft, dense feel that helps at the kitchen, and it suits players moving up from control paddles. Opinions split on break-in and power: Pickleball Tech Dude found it stiff at first before it softened, The Pickleball Dad said other testers reported the same, and SupaSenpai, testing the original standard grit version, found it lacking firepower and best as a defensive paddle. Pickleball Tech Dude gave the Gearbox Draco a slight edge on sweet spot size, while Not Dead Yet Pickleball, testing the elongated Harmony grip version, ranked the Coda above the Selkirk Boomstik and the Enhance MPP Turbo.

Reviewers mostly recommend it as a forgiving control paddle for newer players, with Pickleball Effect citing a large sweet spot and UnforcedErrorsPB suggesting it for players at 3.5 and under. Mixed takes come from power: UnforcedErrorsPB finds enough pop to still put the ball away, while RYE3D Printing finds power muted and says it is not for players wanting power. Pickleball Effect also points players with racket or athletic backgrounds to a different paddle.

Reviewers praise the Friday Aura Pro Widebody for a light swing, and it suits players who want aggressive but not overpowered play. Takes on power and control differ: STS Pickleball measured big power and put control near the bottom of widebodies, while MyPickleList and Pickle Li called power mid-tier with good control and noted dead spots near the handle. Matt's Pickleball finds the response crisp and direct but says resets and drops lose cushion compared with the standard Friday Aura, so touch players may prefer that one.

Reviewers praise the dense, connected feel and large sweet spot, and several point to beginners, newer players and dinkers as the best fit, with All Drive No Drop calling it a good first premium paddle. Power is where takes split: Matt's Pickleball calls drive power strong, All Drive No Drop rates it pretty good but not the highest, and Tickle My Pickleball ranks it lowest for firepower among four widebodies after adding weight. Matt's Pickleball also expects the Gen 3 build to wear out sooner than full foam cores, and says blocks float for passive players.

Reviewers praise the sweet spot, strong baseline power and quiet, soft feel, and several say it suits players who want a standard shape power paddle they can control. The main caution is the break in: STS PICKLEBALL and Pickleball Effect warn that it may keep getting hotter over time, while Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Tech Dude describe a long, stiff start before the sweet spot opens up. Control at the kitchen is mixed, with Derik Hyndman Pickleball finding dinks inconsistent and Pickleball Studio finding spin weaker on dinks, while Johnkew Pickleball found third shot drops, resets and dinks intuitive.

highlights.text: may keep getting hotter over time

paras: Reviewers praise easy dinks, resets and serves, with PickleBALLER finding more control than the Joola Perseus Pro V and Pickleball Playbook liking it for serves, returns, dinks and resets. Power is where takes split: PickleBALLER found the pop lower than the Joola Perseus Pro V, Pickleball Playbook struggled to find drive power and suggested weighted tape, while Pickleball Adventure, testing the 16mm Hyperion, found plenty of pop. PickleBALLER ranked it second of three behind the Joola Kosmos Pro V.

highlights.text: more control than the Joola Perseus Pro V

paras: Reviewers praise the Magnus Pro IV for power, a large sweet spot and stable feel, with Mid-Century Pickleball calling it rock solid and the Pickleheads blog recommending it to forehand-dominant players. The 5-inch handle is the shared complaint, and the Pickleheads video calls it a dealbreaker and would pick another Pro IV paddle, while Mid-Century Pickleball still prefers the 16 mm for singles. Spin splits opinion, since the Pickleheads blog describes topspin that rips but Mid-Century Pickleball rates spin as average to good.

Reviewers liked the wide sweet spot and the control on dinks, resets and drops, with power still there when swung hard. Briones Pickleball Breakdown found the wide body slightly slower through the air, while Johnkew Pickleball found it more muted than an earlier Gen 3 paddle but still a power paddle, and was undecided between the 16mm and 14mm versions. Johnkew Pickleball and Josh J Pickleball both note it is UPA-A certified but not USA Pickleball certified, and Josh J Pickleball is a Joola sponsored professional giving first impressions rather than a full review.

highlights.text: UPA-A certified but not USA Pickleball certified

paras: Minsan Siklista reviews it twice and likes the balanced feel for dinks, resets and attacks, with good dwell and spin, and finds it easier to play than the original Luzz Cannon. Not Dead Yet Pickleball disagrees, saying it hits like a board with no pop, doubting the grit is durable, and not seeing who it suits. Durability is still open, since the 10,000 ball hit claim is unconfirmed and a Minsan Siklista review notes a break in of three weeks to a month with a stiff phase.

highlights.text: easier to play than the original Luzz Cannon

paras: Suits players who want big power and spin and will spend time dialing it in, with DDOG_Pickleball and JJ Pickleball both loving it. Mixed takes come from control, as Matt's Pickleball found it hard to control in competitive play while Famous by Friday Pickleball rated control good once dialed in. Famous by Friday Pickleball also heard a loud, harsh sound and worried about how the ridged core will wear, and some reviewers added weight to the light stock paddle.

highlights.text: hard to control in competitive play

paras: Salt N Pepper Pickleball liked the plush feel, soft touch at the kitchen and arm-friendly vibration damping after adding weight to reach 8.4 ounces, though pure power players may find it too soft. Pickleball Studio and Matt's Pickleball found the stock paddle light and quick but with a small sweet spot that twists on off-center hits, and Matt's Pickleball rates the Ronbus Quanta R3 as the better elongated choice. Pickleball Studio got its best results on the Ronbus Quanta R2 widebody rather than the R1, where a lighter 10 g setup did not do nearly as much, while Matt's Pickleball found about 7 to 8 g of tape per side improved stability and power.

Reviewers praise the power and gritty surface, and it suits players who can center the ball and want extra aggression. Matt's Pickleball was the mixed voice, finding it less forgiving on off-center resets and better with added weight at 3 and 9 o'clock, while MyPickleList found control good in stock form without added weight. BP2 Pickleball found it more aggressive but less forgiving than the RPM Friction Pro Elongated 16mm, and noted the grit felt unchanged after almost four weeks, while DDOG_Pickleball saw no grit loss after two weeks.

Reviewers praise the power, grit and sweet spot, with MyPickleList and Pickle Li both reporting very few edge hits and high tier power, and Matthew K Pickleball calling it a power paddle that can be controlled. The main criticism is pop at the kitchen: Drill More Pickleball finds popups common up close, and MyPickleList and Pickle Li say resets sit a little high. Matthew K Pickleball prefers it over the RPM Q2 Hybrid Curve Top, while Pickleball Advocate prefers the rounded top personally, though a partner coming from an elongated paddle liked the flat top more.

Reviewers mostly suggest it for players who want power from a 13mm paddle, such as rising beginners, early intermediates or anyone after a first paddle, and Pickleball Pirates describes a plush feel with great pop and quick hands at the net. Takes turn mixed on stability: Briones Pickleball Breakdown found the sweet spot small and the paddle not very forgiving, and Pickleheads noted an unstable feel when defending hard drives. Pickleball Blast ranked it D tier after very little court time, calling the 13mm build a harsh starting point for a budget paddle.

highlights.text: unstable feel when defending hard drives

paras: Reviewers like the Odyssey as an affordable, plush, controllable paddle, with Pickleball Medicine and Tickle My Pickleball both placing it in the control leaning all court group, and Farmer Lanky Pickleball and Tickle My Pickleball calling it great value. Takes differ on the sweet spot and pop: STS PICKLEBALL found a smaller Gen 1 sweet spot, Farmer Lanky Pickleball found it average and a little better than the Vatic Pro Prism Flash, and The Pickleball Reviews reported that the 4.5+ players in testing found enough pop for full swings. Pickleball Medicine and Farmer Lanky Pickleball suggest adding weight for more pop and power.

Reviewers praise the Perma Grit spin and suit it to stronger players who already like weighted paddles, with Smash Pickleball liking spin on slow dinks and Maiko liking the strong plow through. Weight is where the takes spread out: Smash Pickleball measured a swing weight of 122, The Sweet Spot 122 to 124 and Maiko 135, and Smash Pickleball and Maiko both found it heavy and slow at the kitchen over longer play. The Sweet Spot prefers the rougher surface of the Spartus Spitfire, finds pop fades after break-in and says the sticky grit suits heat poorly, while Smash Pickleball finds more pop than on the Spartus P1 Hybrid.

Reviewers praise the Phoenix HX for large power and pop in a maneuverable hybrid shape, and it suits players at 4.0 and above who want power over finesse. Takes are mixed on spin, with Pickleball Tech Dude and Pickleball Pursuit reporting good to great spin while Matt's Pickleball finds it low, and on sweet spot size, which Farmer Lanky Pickleball rates as one of the better 14 mm ones but Pickleball Tech Dude calls tight. Resets and dinks are the common complaint, which The Pickleball Dad and Pickleball Pursuit both found hard to control.

Reviewers mostly praise it as an all-court leaning paddle with dwell, touch and a sweet spot that Pickleball Tech Dude finds much larger than on other cutout foam paddles. Power is where takes differ: Dinking And Driving found it hot enough that opponents asked about illegal paddles, while All Drive No Drop Pickleball says it takes a bit more effort to finish points than top power paddles do. Dinking And Driving disliked only the busy graphics, while Tickle My Pickleball found it solid but not exciting.

highlights.text: dwell, touch and a sweet spot

paras: Reviewers describe a quick, punchy paddle for aggressive or advanced players who want fast hands at the net and plenty of pop. Rylie's Review, UnforcedErrorsPB and Pickleball Tech Dude found the sweet spot stable or large, while Pickleball Rx, Johnkew Pickleball and Matt's Pickleball reported an uneven face, extra twisting or jarring off-centre hits. Pickleball Rx and Johnkew Pickleball both preferred the Holbrook Fuze Elongated 16mm for softer, more forgiving contact, and Rylie's Review and UnforcedErrorsPB both noted a break-in period.

Reviewers mostly praise a big sweet spot, good stability and soft, forgiving contact that suits resets and dinks, and several prefer it to the Holbrook Fuze Elongated 14mm. Pickleball Tech Dude was the main dissenter on control, struggling with mid-court control and judging exit speed on resets, while Matt's Pickleball called the elongated shapes niche and several others said the feel needs a few sessions to break in. Power is the least settled point, ranging from low to mid in Pickleball Rx to high in Pickleball Tech Dude and top tier in Pickleball Pursuit.

highlights.text: needs a few sessions to break in

paras: Reviewers liked the hybrid for its power and pop, with Pickleball Tech Dude finding the sweet spot large and stable and Pickleball Pursuit praising its stability. Feel is where takes differ: Pickleball Tech Dude described it as soft and very muted, while Pickleball Pursuit and Matt's Pickleball found it bouncier, or stiffer and more hollow. Three reviewers said it takes some time to learn, and Matt's Pickleball found the light stock paddle better with a few grams of added weight.

highlights.text: better with a few grams of added weight

paras: Martin Grunin Pickleball and JJ Pickleball both prefer this 14mm over the 16mm version, praising easier drops and dinks and good spin, with JJ Pickleball also rating touch at the net highly, at the cost of slightly less power. MaxLevelPickleball is more mixed, finding it too hard to control in doubles for most players unless they drill a lot or play at 5.0 plus, with more pop ups on blocks and resets than the Joola Perseus Gen 3. That reviewer also measured it slightly more powerful than the Joola Perseus Gen 3 in two of three runs, by only one or two mph.

highlights.text: too hard to control in doubles

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the Havik 2 for strong spin, pop and a low swing weight that gives an elongated shape quick hands, with Matt's Pickleball, Cody Childers and Pickleball Blast all pointing to maneuverability at the kitchen. Takes split on the sweet spot: SupaSenpai calls the whole face good, while The Pickleball Pirates found off center hits unforgiving and Matt's Pickleball found the top corners punish high contact. WhiskyDink found it a little softer and denser than the Nox X-Foam Goldin 14mm but not matching their feel profile, and several reviewers add weight to steady it.

highlights.text: strong spin, pop and a low swing weight

paras: Three of four reviewers loved the Joy S+, and it suits players who want a hybrid that plays close to a widebody. Tickle My Pickleball and DDOG_Pickleball both found a better, bigger sweet spot than the Pickleball Apes Joy S, and WhiskyDink liked the robust twist weight, though they and Tickle My Pickleball noted a stiffer feel than the brand's recent softer paddles. Pickleball Pursuit disagreed sharply, calling the feel the worst in a year with a tight sweet spot and below-average stability, while DDOG_Pickleball found it a little light and wanted added weight.

Reviewers who like a stiff paddle get the most from the Joy S, with Pickleball Blast finding good power and pop and a different feel for the budget end. Takes split on the sweet spot: DDOG_Pickleball found it more refined and higher on the face than on the Pickleball Apes Harmony S and Pickleball Apes Charm S, while Tickle My Pickleball found it well below average, with jarring off-center hits. Pickleball Blast found it too stiff in limited play, Tickle My Pickleball said it plushes up with play, and both Tickle My Pickleball and DDOG_Pickleball point to added weight as a fix or plan.

Reviewers who liked it point to spin, power and plow-through in a light, nimble elongated shape that takes added weight well. Mixed takes come from the touch game: Matt's Pickleball says drops need softer hands and that it amplifies high pop issues, and Pickleball Pursuit calls it a power paddle that is harder for players who struggle with resets and dinks, while Famous by Friday Pickleball lists no complaints. Against the Thrive Fury Hybrid 15.5mm, The Sweet Spot Pickleball finds a smaller sweet spot and slower hands, though Famous by Friday Pickleball recorded serve speeds almost level.

highlights.text: smaller sweet spot and slower hands

paras: Reviewers praise the soft, plush feel at the kitchen, where dinks, resets and soft shots are easy to place, and they see it suiting beginners, intermediates and control oriented players. Opinions split on power: Pickle Pick finds it a nice middle ground with no trouble on putaways, while RYE3D Printing finds little pop off the face, with the ball stalling at mid court on a normal swing, and Pickleball Medicine feels behind when opponents speed up. Both testers in the RYE3D Printing review preferred it for dinks.

highlights.text: soft, plush feel at the kitchen

paras: Reviewers like the Psycho for fast, maneuverable hands and a balanced feel with enough pop to stay aggressive without losing control. Salt N Pepper Pickleball calls it a sleeper overshadowed by other Bread & Butter paddles and likes the grabby spin and kitchen control, while Pickleball Blast and Tickle My Pickleball say it works stock but runs light and improves with a little added weight. Tickle My Pickleball adds that it gives up control, plushness and sweet spot stability compared with a 16mm widebody, in return for more pop on drives.

Reviewers say it suits hard hitters who want power from the baseline and quick blocks and counters, and sorrylee Pickleball and Pickleball Playbook both point it at singles players or big swingers. The catch shows up on soft shots: Pickleball Tech Dude struggles to keep passive drops and resets low in stock form, Pickleball Playbook finds resets pop up, and sorrylee Pickleball finds it clearly heavier at the kitchen than the CRBN⁴ TruFoam Barrage, which they would pick for doubles. Spin is judged differently, with sorrylee Pickleball saying it meets expectations and Pickleball Playbook calling it average to below average for a carbon face.

Reviewers praise the soft, dense feel and extra dwell that make dinks, drops and resets easy, and recommend it for doubles players, control players and budget buyers. The main split is with the Friday Aura Pro Elongated: The New Main Pickleball, Dwell Time Pickleball, PickleBaller, Limitless Pickleball and Matt's Pickleball all describe the Aura as the softer control choice, with less power and pop or a less crisp response than that paddle. Pickleheads was the outlier, finding spin the standout but drops and dinks going into the net, and recommends demoing first.

highlights.text: soft, dense feel and extra dwell

paras: Reviewers recommend it for a wide range of players, from beginners to some advanced, who value control, consistency and a big sweet spot over raw power. Pickleball Pursuit and Pickleball Playbook call the firepower modest, and Tickle My Pickleball places it in the middle of the all court foam group, with a smooth, dense, muted feel. Reviewers describe benefits from adding weight, and Pickleball Playbook found the hybrid less stable on resets than the other shapes.

highlights.text: control, consistency and a big sweet spot

paras: Reviewers praise the plush, forgiving feel and good spin from the raw carbon face, and recommend it as an affordable elongated paddle for players moving up to a bit more firepower or doubles players who want spin and touch. Takes split on spin and sweet spot: Tickle My Pickleball and Pickleheads found the spin great, while West Side Pickleball found it lacking, and Famous by Friday Pickleball and West Side Pickleball found the sweet spot only adequate or middling where Pickleheads found it big. Several reviewers, including Pickleball Studio, All Drive No Drop Pickleball and Tickle My Pickleball, say the light stock weight needs added tape.

highlights.text: plush, forgiving feel and good spin
light stock weight needs added tape

paras: Reviewers describe it as plush and the most forgiving of the three GX2 shapes, with a muted feel, fast hand speed and easy resets, and Matt's Pickleball called it a personal favorite for hand exchanges. Takes differ on power: Tickle My Pickleball found the ball comes off faster than the soft feel suggests and called the feel strange, while Pickleball Studio found it all court at best and said units varied between testers. Matt's Pickleball and Pickleball Studio both describe the impact as very muted, and Matt's Pickleball says the near silent sound removes cues for finding the sweet spot.

highlights.text: most forgiving of the three GX2 shapes
cues for finding the sweet spot

paras: PickleTip, Pickleheads and Pickleball Effect describe an elongated shape built for reach and power on full swings, with Pickleheads noting immediate pop and heavy topspin from its NanoBond grit. Pickleball Effect measured the highest max serve speed of the three Pro shapes but the lowest punch volley pop, and PickleTip likewise says quicker paddles feel better when the next ball comes at the body. Matthew K Pickleball finds it feels like an earlier paddle with a smoother feel and no clank at contact, while Pickleheads says the medium stock sweet spot benefits from lead tape.

highlights.text: reach and power on full swings

paras: Dwell Time Pickleball, Pickleball Studio and Matt's Pickleball like the widebody R2 for fast hands and a forgiving shape once weighted, and call it much better value than the power paddles it chases. Stock it disappoints: Pickleball Studio found it unstable with a small sweet spot, and Matt's Pickleball called it thin and hollow, so reviewers advise about 15 g of tape in total or 6 to 8 g on each side. Against the Selkirk LABS Project Boomstik Widebody, Pickleball Studio found drive speed essentially identical with slightly less pop on the Quanta.

highlights.text: unstable with a small sweet spot

paras: Reviewers describe a plush, control leaning paddle, with Pickleball Medicine and Farmer Lanky Pickleball suiting it to players who want control and a soft game, and Tickle My Pickleball expecting the core to be more durable than thermoformed cores. The shared concern is power and stability: all three found pop modest to below average, and Tickle My Pickleball and Farmer Lanky Pickleball flagged the low twist weight, which Farmer Lanky Pickleball says tungsten tape can fix. Pickleball Medicine and Farmer Lanky Pickleball place it above the Vatic Pro Prism Flash on pop, and Farmer Lanky Pickleball leans toward the Spartus Odyssey APEX personally.

Reviewers praise the P1 Standard as a stable, forgiving widebody with durable spin: Pickleball Effect called it one of the most complete widebody paddles available, and Drill More Pickleball made it their main paddle after 200 plus games. Pickleball Adventure was more mixed, finding the spin milder than other long lasting grits and preferring a lighter, faster paddle. Weight is the shared caveat, with swing weights measured from just above 110 to about 115.

highlights.text: milder than other long lasting grits

paras: Reviewers praise the quick hands, the good sweet spot and the easy dinks, drops and resets of this hybrid shape, with a feel several describe as slightly stiffer than the Bread & Butter Shogun. Takes on power differ: Scooter Reviews Stuff finds significantly more pop than the Bread & Butter Shogun, while JJ Pickleball calls power and pop average and Pickleball Pursuit finds moderate power. Tickle My Pickleball and JJ Pickleball both find more power on the Bread & Butter Shogun.

Reviewers praise the plush, springy feel and a good sweet spot, and Pickleball Studio calls it one of the most textbook all court paddles in a while, though without standout power. Opinions on how it compares with the brand's earlier elongated paddle differ: Pickleball Medicine finds more power and a bigger sweet spot, while Farmer Lanky Pickleball finds slightly less power and pop and easier control. Drops settled after about a week for Pickleball Studio and after a few weeks for Daniel Pickleball.

Reviewers like the stability, the large sweet spot and the quick hands of this Kevlar face hybrid, and Pickleball Effect prefers it to the CRBN⁴ TruFoam Genesis for control and firepower. Takes on pop differ: STS PICKLEBALL finds a little more pop and less control than the carbon face Honolulu J2NF, while Matt's Pickleball finds it denser and more muted, without the pop of the Honolulu J2NF. Matthew K Pickleball and Pickleball Medicine both expect the Kevlar face to soften with play.

Reviewers praise the hard hitting power, pop and spin, and Johnkew Pickleball and Pickleball Studio both find it plays much like an earlier delisted paddle, while Dink Kagè Pickleball recommends it for aggressive players with big, quick swings. Control is where takes split: Kev Knows Pickleball cannot recommend it below a 4.0 level and STS PICKLEBALL calls it very hard to control, while Johnkew Pickleball finds control surprisingly decent for this much power. STS PICKLEBALL, Johnkew Pickleball and Pickleball Studio all raise the risk of the core breaking down or crushing.

highlights.text: hard hitting power, pop and spin

paras: Womack Pickleball praises the softer feel and easier control, and UnforcedErrorsPB finds it stable on blocks and resets. SupaSenpai, Pickleball Playbook Paddles and Dinking And Driving still prefer its predecessor, while Pickleball Willy rates it highly and Pickle Li would pick it for the extra dwell. Pickleball On Call measures spin loss after 10 hours, and Amir's Pickleball expects it to wear like raw carbon.

Reviewers praise the spin, the large sweet spot and the controllable power of this elongated foam paddle, and Pickleball Rx finds it more precise on drops and drives than a paddle with more kitchen pace. Feel is where takes split: Matt's Pickleball finds it plush and absorbent, while SupaSenpai and Famous by Friday Pickleball find it dense and stiff with little dwell. Pickleball Tech Dude puts power at the low end, and The Sweet Spot Pickleball places it between low and mid tier.

Reviewers praise the mix of pop and a solid, comfortable feel, and Pickleball Rx rates power as top tier and recommends it from 3.5 up, while Salt N Pepper Pickleball suits it to players around 3.0 and up with good fundamentals. The Sweet Spot Pickleball disagrees on power, placing it at mid tier and finding nothing that stands out. Face texture draws mixed comments: Salt N Pepper Pickleball says the raw carbon grabs the ball, while Pickleball Rx and The Sweet Spot Pickleball find little to no grit or only okay grit.

Reviewers praise the pop on counters and the fast hands, and Matt's Pickleball adds a big sweet spot, calling it the hands frame next to the Nox X-Foam JC6 16mm. Farmer Lanky Pickleball is cooler, rating power as middle of the road, the sweet spot as average for a 16 mm foam paddle and control as hard for anyone below 4.0, with grit that is not the extra durable kind. Matt's Pickleball and Tickle My Pickleball both point to the short handle, and Tickle My Pickleball also dislikes the curved hybrid shape.

Reviewers praise the pace, the stable feel at the kitchen line and the sweet spot, with Cody Childers playing it without any added weight. Pickleball Studio finds it stiffer than the Joola Perseus Pro IV with louder, more aggressive pop that makes resets harder, while Pickleball Pursuit and JJ Pickleball find resets and drops predictable. Pickleball Studio also heard a rattle in both units and notes a six month warranty.

highlights.text: stable feel at the kitchen line

paras: Reviewers praise the dense feel, the spin and the durable grit, and Matt's Pickleball and Pickleball Effect both measured little grit loss after wear. Feel and pop vary: Tickle My Pickleball finds it stiffer and a little less poppy than the Thrive Fury Hybrid, while Farmer Lanky Pickleball finds usable pop that may overwhelm players rated below 3.75. Pickleball Pursuit and The Sweet Spot Pickleball both note a lot of feedback on mishits.

highlights.text: a lot of feedback on mishits

paras: Reviewers praise the hand speed at the net, the spin and a sweet spot that holds up for a 14 mm core. Farmer Lanky Pickleball finds a little less power than the Volair Mach 2 Forza 16mm, and both they and STS PICKLEBALL find more pop from the thinner paddle, while Pickleball Effect finds resets a little less solid. Matthew K Pickleball and Pickleball Effect both needed added weight to bring it under control.

Reviewers praise the huge, forgiving sweet spot, control and spin of this widebody shape, with STS PICKLEBALL naming it the best control paddle in testing. Matthew K Pickleball finds enough power to serve deep and hit from the baseline, while Farmer Lanky Pickleball calls it one of the least powerful Gen 2 raw carbon paddles played. Both Matthew K Pickleball and Pickleball Effect say the sweet spot sits lower, with Matthew K Pickleball warning about tip mishits and Pickleball Effect saying the paddle feels shorter.

Reviewers who liked it praise the fast hands and hand battles at the kitchen, and say it suits higher level players who can place the ball and make their own power. Takes split on feel: some find it stiffer and less forgiving than the Luzz Inferno, with off-center hits that feel harsh, while others like the calm control and shaping and add weight to widen the sweet spot. Several reviewers say the Luzz Inferno is the safer pick for most players.

highlights.text: stiffer and less forgiving than the Luzz Inferno

paras: Reviewers who liked it praise the spin, reach and soft, dense feel, and say it suits players who create their own pace and want easy resets. The sweet spot is the common complaint, with the lowest twist weight in the line and one reviewer who kept shanking the top corners. Takes differ on control, since one reviewer calls it low-tier all-court rather than a control paddle, and others point to the 11SIX24 Hurache-X Power 2 for more reactive pop.

highlights.text: lowest twist weight in the line

paras: Reviewers mostly call it the best Luzz Inferno so far, praising more spin, a wide sweet spot and pop that is easier to predict than on the original Luzz Inferno. Disagreements are about feel and power: one reviewer finds stock stability lower than on the Luzz Inferno Frozen, another finds it poppier with less dwell than the Luzz Inferno, and one finds the original has slightly higher top end power. Most reviewers say grit durability is still unproven.

highlights.text: more spin, a wide sweet spot

paras: Reviewers praise the fast hands, wide sweet spot and easy pop, and recommend it to intermediate and higher level players who can keep the ball down. Most reviewers prefer it to the elongated Aireo Cyclone for stability and speed, though one puts the elongated slightly ahead for power and whip. Grit is the open question: one lab test found the roughness dropped about 23% over 30 hours of play, while another reviewer says the Nanograph surface lasts about twice as long as carbon fiber.

Reviewers like the fast hands, spin and firm, predictable feel, and say it suits players who want an offense first paddle for counters and hand battles. It is called a clear step up in firepower over earlier TruFoam models and the most forgiving yet, but the sweet spot still falls off toward the edges and gets a slight edge to the softer Volair Shift. Three reviewers question the value, with one noting that cheaper rivals match the performance, and one warns off players who want a soft, pocketing feel.

highlights.text: fast hands, spin and firm, predictable feel
sweet spot still falls off toward the edges

paras: Reviewers praise the easy, consistent power and wide sweet spot, and say it suits advanced players who want pace without a heavy swing. Takes differ on touch: one finds blocks and soft drops harder to control, another says resets and blocks came off hotter than wanted before break-in, and a third warns against it for players who want dwell or big spin numbers. None of the three has confirmed how well the grit lasts.

highlights.text: finds blocks and soft drops harder to control

paras: Reviewers who liked it praise the soft, dense feel, ball dwell and comfort on drops, resets and dinks, and say it suits players who like a plush face with pace underneath. Power is where takes split: one reviewer calls it a power paddle with the best spin in the series, another puts it at the bottom of the power category, and a third calls it too muted for pure bangers. Control splits takes too, since one reviewer hit balls long and left resets high, while another finds it reliable with an above average sweet spot, and a third finds it noticeably head heavy with some wrist fatigue.

Reviewers who like it praise power that arrives with a soft, dense feel and without hollow feedback, and say it suits mid to higher level players who want reach on drives and serves. Takes differ on tuning: one reviewer prefers it stock, another says it needs weight at 3 and 9 o'clock to show its potential, and a third advises modest added weight there. The grit is rated Tier 3, a step up from raw carbon fiber but short of the best durable surfaces, and one reviewer calls this the least forgiving shape in the line.

highlights.text: power that arrives with a soft, dense feel

paras: Two reviewers pick it as the best balanced Quanta Pro shape, and say it suits all-court players who want stability and plow through without losing control. The disagreements are mild: one reviewer finds the head shape less confidence-inspiring than the other two Pro shapes, and another says players who need the fastest hands may prefer the standard Quanta. Grit gets a Tier 3 rating from one reviewer, better than raw carbon but behind the best durable surfaces.

Reviewers say it suits aggressive players who want fast, poppy contact, with strong counters and putaways, and some find the sweet spot generous. Feel is where takes split: one reviewer finds it soft and plush with good dwell, another finds a stiff face with no amazing dwell, and a third calls it soft and hollow rather than dense and plush. Two reviewers expect the MAGMAGRIT grit to last, but none has had enough hours on it to confirm.

highlights.text: a stiff face with no amazing dwell

paras: Reviewers who liked it praise the excellent control and touch on soft shots and a plush feel, and say it suits intermediates, tennis converts and all-court recreational players. Takes split on the sweet spot and break-in: one reviewer found it larger over several weeks with mishits staying playable, while another says it needs break-in and feels harsh on off-center hits. Two reviewers suggest adding weight for more plow through and power.

Reviewers mostly praise it as a versatile, controllable all-rounder with a dry medium feel, mainly for intermediate and advanced players. Power is where takes split: Extreme Padel finds it clearly more powerful in smashes than the 2025 model but much less tolerant off centre, while Setup Padel | Mario Pazos calls it the least powerful in the Proline range. Against the Vertex 05 Geo, Fabio Ferro favours the standard model for control and spin, while Extreme Padel would keep the Geo.

highlights.text: least powerful in the Proline range

paras: Reviewers praise the easy handling, wide sweet spot and control, with padelwithmax and Peter Consuegra both describing a softer feel than the 12K. Power is where takes split: Padel Review finds it stiffer and more powerful than the 12K at high swing speeds, while Super Padel Bros finds power and spin lacking. Price draws criticism too, with Fabio Ferro calling it too expensive and suggesting the cheaper 2025 model.

Reviewers praise the control, a dry medium-hard feel and a wide sweet spot, and see it suiting intermediate to advanced players with good technique. Power is where takes split: Trypadel calls it a 100 percent control racket where hitting hard needs a full swing, while Padel Test calls it the most powerful round racket they have tested, though below the Adidas Metalbone HRD. Hotel Palas finds the sweet spot smaller than the standard Endure and prefers that racket, while Mejora Tu Padel picks the Pro over the standard version for personal use.

highlights.text: hitting hard needs a full swing
sweet spot smaller than the standard Endure

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the control, the easy power on smashes, bandeja and volleys, and a comfortable, manoeuvrable feel, and it suits intermediate to advanced attacking players. Power is where takes split: Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel and PadelLab find it more powerful than the standard Vertex 05 in the smash, while Simone Mazzola Padel finds smashes less explosive than a classic Vertex and Extreme Padel finds them leaving slower. Several reviewers, including Probando Palas and Setup Padel | Mario Pazos, also dislike the smooth area near the logo, where the ball slides, and some note the rough texture wears off.

highlights.text: easy power on smashes, bandeja and volleys
more powerful than the standard Vertex 05
less explosive than a classic Vertex

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the easy handling, comfortable feel and touch at the net, and place it with intermediate to advanced players. Power is where takes split: Extreme Padel calls it the clear winner in its smash power test, while Super Padel Bros finds the ball exit weak and the power low. Against the 18K, Padel Elite Barletta finds the 12K gives much more push at high pace, while Probando Palas finds the 18K gives more control from the baseline, and some reviewers call the price too high.

Reviewers mostly point intermediate and advanced players to it for control with extra attacking response, and volleys, vibora and smashes are the most praised areas. Probando Palas finds it more powerful than the standard Neuron 02 but less manoeuvrable from the baseline, while el4Set finds it very light with the best defensive control they remember testing and weak smashes, which goes against what most reviewers say about finishing. Nmscontrolpadel calls the sweet spot small and notes vibration on off-centre hits, and Dani 13 finds balls come out shorter when hit away from the middle.

Reviewers mostly praise the spin from the rough surface, easy maneuverability and attacking potential, and see it as suiting technical or offensive players. Canary Padel calls it one of the most balanced rackets of the year for a wide audience, while Simone Mazzola Padel finds control only inside a smaller sweet spot and would not buy it. Reviewers also differ on feel against last year, with Probando Palas finding it softer than the 2025 and Otro Nivel Padel and Dani 13 finding it harder than last year's version.

highlights.text: one of the most balanced rackets

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the 2026 Metalbone 3.5 for smash and overhead power, with a removable weight system, and recommend it to advanced and upper intermediate players. Padel Smash TV finds it easier to control than the HRD Plus, while Extreme Padel finds it more forgiving than the HRD+ but still demanding and tiring at the net. Simone Mazzola Padel and Fabio Ferro both see little change from the 3.4 and question the price, with Fabio Ferro preferring the Metalbone Carbon.

Reviewers praise the power on smashes and víboras, along with a sweet spot that is larger than standard, and several point to attacking players with good technique and fitness. Probando Palas suggests it suits less advanced players who want easy power, while Extreme Padel recommends level 7 minimum and felt it in the shoulder after 20 minutes. Dani13 finds the Coello Motion better for defence and volleys, and Simone Mazzola Padel finds the Pro heavy at the net and less powerful than the Delta Pro.

highlights.text: sweet spot that is larger than standard

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the Xplo 2026 for volleys and net play, with Padel Racket Australia describing a firm, direct feel and Padel5 describing power without losing control, and it is generally aimed at advanced or medium to high level players. Opinions split on the sweet spot and spin, as Otro Nivel / Justpadel finds a very big sweet spot and a lot of spin, while the4Set finds the sweet spot smaller than the Neuron Edge and the glossy surface harder for spin shots. Weight and demands are the other catch, since Otro Nivel / Justpadel calls it heavy at 365 to 375 g and Padel Racket Australia says late or off-center contact is punished.

highlights.text: glossy surface harder for spin shots

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the control, manoeuvrability and secure volleys, and suit it to players who build points rather than rely on power. Spin is where they split: Padel Review scores it 6.5 and dislikes the lack of spin, while Fabio Ferro scores spin 8.5. Several reviewers, including Extreme Padel and Probando Palas, point players wanting more power to the Neuron 02 Edge, and Fabio Ferro calls the price high.

highlights.text: more power to the Neuron 02 Edge

paras: Reviewers praise the HRD+ for smash power and stable volley blocks, and rate it for advanced attacking players, with some saying it fits the left side best. Opinions split on handling and forgiveness: Simone Mazzola Padel finds defence better than expected with a good sweet spot, while Extreme Padel finds it more demanding than the standard Metalbone and Tom Pandore says it left them late on fast balls. Hotel Palas picks it over the standard 3.5 for control on blocks, and several reviewers prefer it with the weights removed.

highlights.text: more demanding than the standard Metalbone

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the spin from the rough texture and the easy handling for a diamond shape, and place it with advanced or aggressive players, often on the left side. Power is where takes split: Padel5 finds smashes go like a cannon, while Simone Mazzola Padel and Padel Review find the power less extreme than expected. Mejora Tu Padel and the4Set are mixed, with Mejora Tu Padel seeing little difference from the regular Defy and the ball rising in defense, and the4Set struggling to feel the ball on lobs.

highlights.text: easy handling for a diamond shape
the power less extreme than expected
struggling to feel the ball on lobs

paras: Reviewers who liked it, mostly advanced and intermediate-high players who want power, praise the dry touch and the easy handling for an offensive racket at roughly 360 to 366 g. Mixed takes come from the Soft name: Mejora Tu Padel calls it a hard racket that is only a little more flexible than the standard 3.0, and Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel finds it only slightly more forgiving than the regular Viper, while pdhsports finds it much softer than the older Technical range. Dani 13 says off-centre balls die, and the4Set reports less control at high speed and on volleys than the hard version.

highlights.text: easy handling for an offensive racket

paras: Reviewers mostly praise strong power on smashes and fast attacking shots, and say it suits experienced or advanced players with good physical condition. Reported weights range from 366 g to 378 g, and reviewers describe it as heavy and hard to handle, with a small sweet spot and little ball output. Dani 13 rates control as very good, while Mejora Tu Padel finds low volleys float in transition play, and Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel prefers the Soft version in defence.

Reviewers mostly praise its control and easy handling, and it suits players who want a dry, predictable feel and build points rather than finish them. Sweet spot size is where opinions split: Simone Mazzola Padel finds the sweet spot not generous and the racket demanding, while Nico Ballesteros rates it as huge and forgiving compared with the Attack version. Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel finds it the stiffest and driest next to the AT10 12K and AT10 18K and harder on the arm, and Extreme Padel and el4Set both place its power below the Attack or the Genius 12K.

Reviewers praise the Endure V1 as a balanced round racket with good control and precision, suited to intermediate players and to those moving up to a first advanced racket. Mixed takes come mostly from comparisons with the Pro: Mejora Tu Padel finds it more manoeuvrable but with less body, and Justpadel finds smashes can kick out and would pick the Pro for power. Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel names it the most balanced of the three Endure models, though it is only correct on smashes.

Reviewers mostly praise it as a middle step between the Coello Pro and the Coello Team, with power that is easier to handle than the Pro, and some aim it at intermediate to advanced players. Simone Mazzola Padel finds it a softer Pro that is not different enough to justify a separate model, and calls it demanding to move at the net. Extreme Padel calls it head heavy with a reduced sweet spot, and Tino finds the sweet spot smaller and limits sessions to two hours.

highlights.text: easier to handle than the Pro
demanding to move at the net
head heavy with a reduced sweet spot

paras: Reviewers mostly describe an attacking diamond racket for intermediate to advanced players, praising its control at pace, viper shots and volleys. Opinions split on how it compares with other rackets: Peter Consuegra finds it clearly behind the Vertex 04 for control, while Rodri Ovide switched from the Vertex to the Hack. Sweet spot size also varies, with Padel Test by Roberto Cardi finding it high and not very wide, and Padel Review finding it bigger than on previous Hacks.

Reviewers praise the grip on the ball and spin from the 3D sandy surface, along with a wide sweet spot, for intermediate to advanced players. Sweet spot opinions differ: Extreme Padel finds it restricted and vibrating off centre, while Mejora Tu Padel calls it very wide. Padel Vlog Italia finds it more playable than the V2 and V2.5, but Padel Review prefers the older 2.5 and Padel Test by Roberto Cardi gives only 5.5 out of 10 for value.

Reviewers praise the soft, precise touch and the side weights that shift the balance between control and power. Simone Mazzola Padel calls it a builder's racket rather than a finisher and rates the price as very high, while Otro Nivel Padel finds it less powerful on the kick smash and heavier in defense than the Arrow Hit Control, though softer and less trampoline than the Metalbone Control. Padel House finds ball speed comes easily and recommends it to players with good technique, but warns that forcing the shot at the net can cost control.

highlights.text: side weights that shift the balance
forcing the shot at the net can cost control

paras: Reviewers recommend it mainly to intermediate and advanced players who like to attack, praising smash and viper power, with Padel Review and Practica Padel Team also noting no arm vibration. Takes split on handling: Conect Padel finds it more manoeuvrable in defence than expected and Padel Test by Roberto Cardi finds it easier than the Metalbone HRD, while Dani 13 finds handling worse than last year and Fabio Ferro finds it head-heavy and tiring. Several reviewers, including Padel Review and Practica Padel Team, find the sweet spot small and call the removable weight system too complicated, so both advise playing without weights.

Reviewers mostly praise the control and quick handling, and several recommend it to intermediate players who want a controlled, flat game, with Conect Padel calling it very recommendable for defensive players. Sweet spot opinions differ: PadelHQ calls it generous, while Dani 13 says off-center hits feel dry and Hotel Palas finds it narrower than the standard Metalbone CTRL, which it split two to two in a head to head. Power is the common limit, as Padel Review finds power drops as pace rises and Practica Padel Team scores smashes 6 out of 10.

Reviewers praise the large sweet spot and soft, comfortable feel, and Otro Nivel Padel calls it one of the best round rackets on the market, suited to intermediate and pro players. Power is where takes split: Tino finds it a bit too safe at the net and points to the standard Metalbone for explosive attacks, while Dani 13 calls it the most powerful control shape at this hardness but finds the volley zone slower with the Weight and Balance screws. Otro Nivel Padel also finds the Metalbone and Metalbone Hard more powerful, though with a smaller sweet spot.

highlights.text: a bit too safe at the net

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the round Metalbone CTRL 3.4 for a wide, central sweet spot, easy handling and comfort, with some noting no vibration. Mixed takes come from power and price: Dani 13 finds it bouncy at fast pace and well behind the normal Metalbone and Hard for flat smashes, Padel Review finds flat smashes lack punch, and Padel Test by Roberto Cardi calls the price too high. Fabio Ferro rates it easier to play than the 3.4 HRD but still prefers the HRD overall, while PadelCritic gives control as its best trait.

Reviewers mostly praise the power, with smashes, volleys and spin mentioned often, and most see it as suited to advanced players, particularly left-side players. Fabio Ferro and Practica Padel Team both find it more solid and powerful than the softer 3.4, though heavier in the head and harder to control. Opinions on the sweet spot differ, as Talk About Padel finds it big while Padel Review finds it smaller than the standard 3.4.

Reviewers praise the light, quick handling and a wider sweet spot than earlier Air Vipers, with good spin from the sandy rough surface. Opinions differ on power: Simone Mazzola Padel finds overhead power lacking at the low weight, while PadelVergleich calls the power impressive but the sweet spot still small. Padel Lovers and Fabio Ferro both prefer it to the Technical Viper 2025, though Padel Lovers warns that weaker technique can still bring short balls.

Reviewers praise the Air Viper 2026 for easy movement and quick net play, and some find it more comfortable and slightly more elastic than the 2025 model. Fabio Ferro finds less control and a late ball exit on volleys when forced. Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel finds it less dry than older versions, and Simone Mazzola Padel sees the sandblasted roughness as a step back from last year.

highlights.text: easy movement and quick net play

paras: Reviewers praise the control, wide sweet spot and spin, and Padel Review and El chini consejo place it with intermediate to advanced players. Feel is where takes differ: El chini consejo finds it harder than the Vertex, Metalbone HRD and AT10 18K Genius, while Probando Palas calls it medium-hard and about half a point harder than the AT10 12K. Padel Review finds 372 g less maneuverable, and Fabio Ferro notes less raw power than the Technical Viper.

highlights.text: control, wide sweet spot and spin
less raw power than the Technical Viper

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as a round control racket for upper-intermediate to advanced players, with stable defence, controlled bandeja and vibora, and a large sweet spot. Dani 13 finds the centred sweet spot slightly smaller and the handling demanding, while Fabio Ferro calls the sweet spot bigger and the feel a little less dry than the 2025 model. Simone Mazzola Padel warns the hard feel is rough on the arm, whereas CONSIGN 77 recommends it to players prone to arm fatigue, and Pádel con Clase sees little change from the 2024 and no extra power.

highlights.text: hard feel is rough on the arm

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the smash and flat-shot power and suit the racket to advanced, aggressive players who bring their own technique. Opinions split on the sweet spot, as PADELARTE calls it wide for an attacking racket while Fabio Ferro rates it the smallest of the Viper sisters. Padel Lovers prefers the Air Viper 2025 as more playable, and Tom Pandore - Padel finds this year's racket much harder and more demanding than the 2024 version.

Reviewers point intermediate and advanced players to it for the Viper shape with a softer, more manageable feel than the regular Viper, and pdhsports adds more forgiveness and a softer feel on the arm. Opinions differ on how soft it really is: Dani 13 rates its hardness at 8 out of 10, while Mejora tupadel calls it the softest of the Lebrón rackets but still a hard racket. Padel Review finds more ball output but a woodier sound and slightly less control than the regular Viper Juan Lebron, and pdhsports finds it harder to get the most from when late on the ball.

highlights.text: a softer feel on the arm

paras: Reviewers praise the control and handling, and Dani 13 and Probando Palas both liken it to the Nox AT10 12K, while Yannick Doston / Tenniszon recommends it to advanced players who want control and forgiveness. Opinions split on the net game: xTRES Padel does not quite like it at the volley and ranks it second to last in a Bullpadel line test, while Probando Palas finds volleys carry good weight at medium rhythm. Dani 13 and Tenniszon both say it is not for power players, and Dani 13 notes the ball can float on the bandeja if the downward gesture is short.

highlights.text: not quite like it at the volley

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the easy handling, control at the net and a slightly wider sweet spot. Power is where takes split: Mellis_YTB rates it 8.5 for power, below the Xplo at 9.5 and the Hack at 9, while Ariel Padel Reviews calls it strong on power for smashes. Reviewers also disagree on the rubber, as the4Set and Ariel Padel Reviews describe new hard EVA while Dani 13 and Hotel Palas say it ships with MultiEva, and Dani 13 does not find the change from last year worth an upgrade.

Reviewers praise the control and quick handling at the net, and two of them place it with upper-intermediate to advanced players rather than those still building technique. Practica Padel Team calls power standard with low ball exit at medium-low pace, while PadelCritic scores power at 8.9 for a low balance racket, so views on how much power it offers differ. Both place the standard Vertex 04 ahead on power, and xTRES Padel also finds less bandeja output than Paquito's racket or Delfi's.

highlights.text: control and quick handling at the net
low ball exit at medium-low pace

paras: Reviewers praise handling and control in a light diamond-shaped racket, and recommend it to attacking or all-round players at intermediate to advanced level. Power is where takes split: Padel Test by Roberto Cardi finds little power from the medium-low balance, while PadelCritic says it gives real pace on smashes and víboras. Padel Review finds it the stiffest Vertex Woman so far, with a smaller sweet spot.

Reviewers mostly praise the smash power and fast ball speed of the 3K carbon face, and see it as suited to intermediate-high or advanced players who attack. Dani 13 finds it more powerful than this year's Neuron in the smash but less forgiving, and Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel finds it more demanding than the 2026 version, with a higher balance that slows defence and volleys. pdhsports calls it the most powerful Bullpadel and more playable than earlier versions, while Ariel Padel Reviews finds it harder to play than earlier versions despite a surprising smash.

highlights.text: smash power and fast ball speed

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as a lighter, more manoeuvrable alternative to the Coello Pro for intermediate and advanced players, with strong smash power. Padel Magazine finds it clearly more manoeuvrable than the Pro but with less power, and one left-side tester keeps the Pro for attack, while Padel Chiquito also rates the Pro as the better choice for attacking. Simone Mazzola Padel finds the sweet spot average, and Padel Test by Roberto Cardi calls the sweet spot not very large and the price too high.

Reviewers praise the light, manoeuvrable handling for a diamond shape, and it suits advanced or mobile attackers, with Stéphane Penso / Padel Magazine and Simone Mazzola Padel both coming away positive. Feel is where takes split: John Macallan / Padelmesh calls it medium-hard, while El chini consejo finds it softer than the Head Delta Motion and less enjoyable. The sweet spot is small according to several reviewers, and Simone Mazzola Padel finds spin below expectations.

Reviewers praise it at the net, with strong blocks, volleys and smashes, and recommend it to advanced players with a trained arm. Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel finds it more manageable and better for ball speed control than the Head Coello Pro, while the4Set finds the Coello Pro slightly more powerful but the Extreme Pro easier on defense. Spin is where takes split, as Padel Test by Roberto Cardi calls the 3D surface exceptional and the4Set lists the spin texture as an area to improve.

highlights.text: spin texture as an area to improve

paras: Reviewers praise the control, precision and placement of this 2026 teardrop, and recommend it to advanced players who build points rather than look for easy power. Probando Palas finds it more reactive and dynamic than the previous Radical Pro with a wide sweet spot, while PADELREVIEW ENG calls the touch as hard as the new Extreme Pro or harder and says it is not the fastest to maneuver.

Reviewers praise easy handling despite the high balance, good ball exit and a forgiving sweet spot, mostly for intermediate and advanced players. Spin is where takes split: Fabio Ferro and Padel Review find the smooth faces give little grip, while Padel Test by Roberto Cardi says cuts bite well. Padel Smash TV prefers it to the Speed Pro for maneuverability, and Mica / padelblend reports arm problems that appeared over time.

highlights.text: easy handling despite the high balance
arm problems that appeared over time

paras: Reviewers praise the quick handling and dry, progressive response, and PadelCritic places it with advanced or established intermediate players rather than beginners. Dani 13 calls the sweet spot wider than most rivals, while Probando Palas and PadelCritic describe it as standard size. Dani 13 finds it less bouncy than a Metalbone Hard but notes that fast volleys can send the ball to the glass, while Probando Palas prefers it to the Power Pro at high speeds.

Reviewers praise the comfort, handling and control of the 2025 model, and it suits players who want a controlled medium feel. Feel is where takes differ: Conect Padel finds it soft with a very wide sweet spot, while PADELARTE describes a hard, dry feel and only a medium sweet spot. Smash power is the most common limit, with Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel and PadelCritic finding smashes less decisive than a diamond racket, though PADELARTE finds much more smash power than in the 2024 version.

highlights.text: less decisive than a diamond racket

paras: Reviewers praise the wide sweet spot, comfort and control, and mostly place it with intermediate to advanced players. Takes differ on the 18K comparison: Conect Padel finds the 12K firmer and in need of more arm push on lobs, while PadelCritic calls the 18K stiffer and the 12K slightly more forgiving. Probando Palas finds it very similar to the 2024 version and dislikes the noticeable edges of the new octagonal grip.

Reviewers mostly praise the quick handling, comfort and control, and they rate it well at the net and in defence. Smash power is where opinions split: Dani 13 finds flat smashes lacking and the ball floating at fast pace, while PADELREVIEW ENG is surprised by the overhead power and Julien / Padel Passion finds power convincing once the swing is committed. Dani 13 also finds it less controlled at fast pace than the AT10 18K, and PADELREVIEW ENG and Julien / Padel Passion both call the price high.

Reviewers praise it as easy to move, and it suits intermediate to advanced players who want a versatile racket that leans toward control. Fabio Ferro calls it the most powerful AT10 in recent years, but finds it stiffer, with less spin, a smaller sweet spot and a very high price, while Peter Consuegra finds more control than attack and less output than the Attack models. Dani 13 finds it forgiving in the volley zone but needs the tip pulled down to stop the ball floating on bandeja and vibora, and both Fabio Ferro and Dani 13 add weights to the head.

highlights.text: most powerful AT10 in recent years

paras: Reviewers praise it as an attacking racket with good volleys, bandeja and vibora, aimed at players who want ball feel and control alongside a high balance. Canary Padel finds it less powerful than the 12K and says it eats the ball a little at high rhythms, and Probando Palas expects the 12K Attack or the EA10 to do better on flat smashes. Peter Consuegra needs about two weeks to adjust to the heavier head, and Padel Market says defence costs a little more because the weight sits toward the tip.

Reviewers praise its control and handling, and place it with intermediate players who build points rather than rely on the smash. Padel Review is the mixed take, calling the price high and finding it unstable at high pace with little smash power. Setup Padel | Mario Pazos loved it and calls it the most powerful racket in the control range, with a dry, firm feel unlike the softer classic ML10, while Padel Market sees it closer to a hybrid with a lot of ball feeling.

Reviewers praise the fast, manoeuvrable handling and the control at the net, and it suits intermediate to advanced players who hit actively. Probando Palas and Fabio Ferro both set it against the Babolat Air Viper, with Probando Palas finding it slightly more direct and controllable and Fabio Ferro noting a touch less ball exit. Sweet spot opinions differ, as PADELREVIEW ENG calls it tiny while Padel Test by Roberto Cardi finds it possibly slightly wider than the 2025, and John Macallan / Padelmesh adds that defence is the weakest area.

Fabio Ferro and Padel Review both loved it as a powerful racket for advanced players, with strong spin, and Padel Review also finds a controlled ball exit. Probando Palas finds the sweet spot more demanding than the Ultimate Pro and prefers the Pro on the baseline, while Dani 13 finds the sweet spot slightly larger than the Babolat Technical Viper 2025 but calls the weight a disadvantage for volleys. Padel Review also notes that the identical Classic version costs less.

Reviewers describe an offensive diamond for intermediate to advanced intermediate players, praised for a forgiving sweet spot, easy handling and controlled volleys. Opinions on movement differ: Probando Palas finds it moves well from the back, while PalaHack says it moves worse than lighter versions of the range. On power, Padel Test by Roberto Cardi places it below the Phenix Pro and Metalbone HRD.

Reviewers praise the firm, direct touch and quick handling, especially for volleys and building points, with intermediate to advanced players the usual target. Padel Test by Roberto Cardi finds the sweet spot wide and forgiving. Otro Nivel Padel and Stéphane Penso / Padel Magazine both describe a more direct touch than the 2025 model, and Dani 13 finds the lower hardness makes fast flat attack need more effort, while several reviewers rate power as moderate.

Reviewers mostly praise it for control, a wide sweet spot and net play, and recommend it to advanced and aggressive players. Handling is where takes split, as Dani 13 finds it very good while Padel Review finds it bulky to move and hard to use in defensive recoveries. Practica Padel Team and Padel Test by Roberto Cardi both find it softer than the Metalbone 3.4, whereas PadelCritic rates comfort and forgiveness at only 8.1 and notes vibration in long sessions.

Reviewers mostly place it with intermediate and advanced players and praise the spin from the sanded face, with several also noting easy handling. The sweet spot is where takes split: Dani 13 and Padel Test by Roberto Cardi find it wide, while Simone Mazzola Padel finds it unforgiving off centre and Fabio Ferro finds it lower than last year. Weight also divides opinion, as Padel Review's 375 g unit was hard to move and tired the arm, while Probando Palas and Padel Test by Roberto Cardi weighed 362 g and 363 g units and found them easy to handle.

highlights.text: 375 g unit was hard to move

paras: Reviewers praise the easy power and the grippy sandy finish, and Dani 13 and Setup Padel | Mario Pazos both point to backhand players as the target. Handling is where opinions split: Dani 13 finds the 369 g unit with a 27.1 cm balance hard to move in defence and volleys, while Setup Padel | Mario Pazos weighs a unit at 361 g with a balance of 27 and finds it moves well. Probando Palas finds it not the best from the back and a step below the Fenix Pro at full power, and Dani 13 finds control weaker than last year's Elite at medium and slow pace.

highlights.text: hard to move in defence and volleys
not the best from the back

paras: Reviewers praise the smash power and spin from the rough surface, and it suits advanced players who attack. Handling is where takes split: Padel Test by Roberto Cardi calls it very manoeuvrable and Simone Mazzola Padel finds it easy to move, while PadelCritic rates manoeuvrability as limited and the sweet spot as the smallest in its comparison. Dani 13 finds it more demanding than the Pro 4 when applying little force, and the stock grip wore out quickly for Padel Review and Simone Mazzola Padel.

Reviewers praise the power, especially on smashes and at the net, and point it at advanced attacking players, with Chingoland rating it probably the best value top signature racket. Opinions on the sweet spot split: Otro Nivel Padel finds it everywhere, while Padel Test by Roberto Cardi finds it small and punishing off-centre. Probando Palas finds it demanding to move from the baseline, and Rens van Rijsewijk / Racketdoktor warns that vibration reaches the arm.

highlights.text: find it small and punishing off-centre
demanding to move from the baseline

paras: Reviewers praise its handling and smash, and several place it with intermediate to advanced or competitive players. Power is where takes split: Stéphane Penso / Padel Magazine rates it close behind the Fenix Pro, while Probando Palas finds it not super powerful at high pace. Padelmesh calls the feel firm and dry with possible arm fatigue, whereas Tino finds it lighter than expected at around 350 grams and easier to control than the Electra Pro.

highlights.text: easier to control than the Electra Pro
not super powerful at high pace

paras: Reviewers praise its net play and overheads, with Padel Review liking the explosive but controllable ball output and Peter Consuegra rating it strong on the víbora and smash. Feel is where opinions split: OngoalSweden finds it softer than StarVie rackets usually feel and more control than power, while Peter Consuegra finds it dry, hard and aimed at high level players. All three note a limited sweet spot, and OngoalSweden finds the Drax Plus gives more speed and forgives off-centre hits better, while Padel Review adds that the small, thin handle needs an overgrip.

highlights.text: strong on the víbora and smash

paras: Reviewers praise the 2024 Bela LT V2.5 as a comfortable, easy-to-handle racket with a good sweet spot, mostly for intermediate players. Power is where takes split: Padel Test by Roberto Cardi finds excellent power, while Padel Review calls it not powerful and the flat smash weak, and Fabio Ferro says the soft core bends under full swings. Against the heavier Bela Pro, Padel FYI finds the Pro punchier but harder to use on low balls at the net.

Reviewers praise the spin and control, and most place it with intermediate players, with PADEL WORLD relaying players who preferred it to the heavier, harder Defy Pro. Sweet spot size is where opinions split: Extreme Padel finds it very small and unforgiving off-centre, while Probando Palas calls it well optimized and Padel Review calls it generous. Power also varies, as Fabio Ferro rates it high and Padel Review calls it only fair.

Reviewers praise its control, precise placement and easy handling, and point it at experienced or confirmed players who want a firm, dry feel. Stéphane Penso / Padel Magazine places it as more accessible than the Vertex 05 and the Geo, while Probando Palas finds it loses a little against the standard Vertex 05 in aerial play and at the net but gains at the back of the court. Power is the main reservation, as Probando Palas points to a lack of easy power.

highlights.text: control, precise placement and easy handling
gains at the back of the court

paras: Reviewers praise the control and balanced feel, and recommend it to intermediate players and above who want a solid but not heavy racket. Simone Mazzola Padel disagrees with the brand's intermediate claim, finds it demanding and sees it suiting advanced attacking players, while Fabio Ferro rates the Ultimate Pro and Pure Pro as more powerful. Probando Palas prefers the Hyper Pro Plus 2026 for harder hitters, and PADELREVIEW ENG calls the Hyper Pro gentle on the arm, whereas Simone Mazzola Padel doubts it suits tennis elbow because of its technical demands.

Reviewers mostly praise the long battery life and low price of this light OLED laptop, from almost 19 hours at 200 nits on the Ryzen 7 350 model (Just Josh) to about 10 hours on the Ryzen AI 7 350 with 32GB (Ryan's Tech Garage). Mixed takes come from speed, since the Ryzen AI 7 350 version has CPU results below last year's Ryzen 7 8840HS and the Intel version (Notebookcheck), while the older Ryzen 7 8840HS model performs almost identically and is the one to buy on sale (Just Josh). The 60Hz screen was a common criticism, with the Ryzen AI 7 350 unit's 1200p panel called dim at about 360 nits and a harder sell than the MacBook Air M4 (Hardware Canucks).

Reviewers praise the ThinkPad keyboard and long battery life, with the Snapdragon X Elite version running roughly 20 hours or more in several light-use tests, and see it as an office laptop. Takes split by config: the Snapdragon model trails the MacBook Pro M3 in Cinebench (Andrew Marc David) and has app and driver gaps, the Ryzen AI 7 Pro 360 version kept its speed under sustained load where the Snapdragon throttled a bit (Notebookcheck), and the Core Ultra 5 228V version ran quieter and cooler but trails AMD and Snapdragon in multi-core (NotebookcheckReviews). The Ryzen 7 Zen 5 version ran extremely hot and loud under load at a price that Just Josh called outrageous, and the 60Hz 1200p screen draws criticism from several reviewers.

highlights.text: extremely hot and loud under load

paras: Reviewers mostly recommend the base 16GB model for its speed and light fanless body, with single-core scores about 21 percent above the M3 Air (Max Tech, Tom's Guide). Takes split on heat and upgrades: Snazzy Labs and Max Tech saw the fanless chassis throttle under sustained load, while 9to5Mac reported no throttling in eight months of everyday use, and Hardware Canucks and Tom's Guide point M1 Air users toward upgrading while M2 or M3 users wait. The 256GB base storage and two ports draw the most criticism (The Verge, 9to5Mac), and Created Tech found the Air a better default than the M4 MacBook Pro.

It suits gamers and creators who want a light, premium 14-inch machine and can live with fan noise and heat, with reviewers praising the OLED screen, speakers and aluminum build. Opinions split on value and comparisons: the 2023 G14 with RTX 4090 stays just ahead of the RTX 5080 version in most tests (Notebookcheck), the 2025 model is almost identical to the 2024 G14, which is cheaper (Crimson Tech), and the Razer Blade 14 is nicer and quieter (PC Gamer). Several reviewers favor the RTX 5070 Ti version over the RTX 5080 version (Josh Craves Tech, PC Gamer, Matthew Moniz), and battery results vary from 10h 27min of web surfing at 150 nits on the RTX 5080 model (Notebookcheck) to 5-6 hours of general use on the RTX 5080 model (Tom's Guide).

highlights.text: OLED screen, speakers and aluminum build

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the body under 1 kg, the keyboard and the OLED, and on the Core Ultra 7 258V version with 32GB several measured longer battery life than the Gen 12 (Notebookcheck, Tom's Hardware). Mixed takes come from price and speed: PCWorld said it trails AMD chips and called the price incredibly expensive, while Laptop Mag found multicore speed a letdown and noted the MacBook Pro 14 M4 lasted 18:32 against 11:28 here. Results on that same configuration still vary, from 16 hours 37 minutes in PCMark 10 (Andrew Marc David) to about 11 hours of web browsing, and Lunar Lake caps RAM at 32GB.

highlights.text: longer battery life than the Gen 12

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as a desk-bound RTX 5090 laptop with strong performance, cool surfaces and an optional Cherry MX keyboard, and Trusted Reviews called it the most powerful gaming laptop they had tested. Mixed takes come from the screen and rivals: the MSI Raider 18 HX AI has a better mini-LED screen (PCMag UK), the Medion Erazer Beast 16 X1 Ultimate is much cheaper with better battery life (Trusted Reviews), and the HP Omen Max 16 came out marginally ahead in most gaming tests (PC Gamer). Battery was short on the RTX 5090 units, such as 1h 58min of web browsing in Notebookcheck's test, and PC Gamer found it cannot run at full power unplugged.

highlights.text: most powerful gaming laptop they had tested
cannot run at full power unplugged

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as a quiet, fast everyday laptop, with the 16GB, 8-core GPU model beating the Dell XPS 13 in Geekbench (Laptop Mag) and lasting 14 hours 41 minutes on a web browsing test. Mixed takes come from heavy work, where Tech Radiator found the 8GB, 256GB model very hot and frustrating for video editing, and Max Tech saw about a 15% Cinebench drop on the 7-core GPU model once it heated up, though it still exported faster than the Intel Air (Max Tech). Against newer chips, everyday speed felt indistinguishable from the M3 or M4 (Created Tech), but the M1 scored 361 in Solar Bay Extreme against 2400 for the M4 Air (Luke Miani).

highlights.text: very hot and frustrating for video editing

paras: Reviewers mostly recommend it to students, commuters and moderate video editors who want a bigger screen in a light, quiet body, with Beebom measuring 13 to 14 hours on its M4 16GB unit and Tom's Guide 15 hours 14 minutes in a web test on its 16GB and 256GB unit. Opinions split on sustained load: Kevin Ferrandiz found the top and keyboard uncomfortably hot in a programming benchmark, though less than on the 13-inch M4 (Kevin Ferrandiz), while The Verge saw throttling in Photoshop and Lightroom Classic and Macwelt measured the M4 MacBook Pro six percent ahead in a stress test thanks to active cooling (Macwelt). Some reviewers see little reason to upgrade from the M3 (Beebom, Tom's Guide, Macwelt), and Tom's Guide calls the 13-inch M4 Air the pick for most people, with this as second choice (Tom's Guide).
